Richardson tn " The Times." It seems to me the most urgent consideration for a tenant farmer is the all important question of "tenure." The best, as well for agricultural as for all other purposes, may be simply and truly stated as that which is as like ownership as it can be made—a long lease, or no lease at all, but a perfect understanding with a liberal-minded landlord (pro- vided he never die) is the next best thing. A man who is simply tenant-at-will, or from year to year, subject to six months' notice only, is not likely to farm well, or to his own or any one's advantage without good and sufficient security for his outlay, much of which will require a round of crop- ping at least, and some of it more, to recoup him for his outlay, as this requires to be renewed from year to year to keep up the fertility of the soil, so that his tenant right on leaving will be large or small, according to his liberal or generous farming. Therefore it is that an agreement or covenant should exist, and signed by both landlord and tenant, to determine the amounts due to the tenant on quit- ting for cake and tillages used, and ether unexhansted and permanent improvements, and the more liberally drawn on the several clauses in the said agreement the more likely the tenant to farm in an enterprising manner, knowing that be holds good and sufficient seeurity for all the improve- ments he may have done for some years back. The precise terms as to amount of allowances will be specified. As for cake one-third for last two years, or one-half for last year and one-third the year before, and perhaps more preferable still, one-third for past three years. Equally liberal should be for tillages and permanent improvements; and for the latter due weight should be given to the regularly kept accounts of outgoing tenants if he has them), in which should be found exact cost of draining and other improve- ments for the pasts seven or even ten years, and amount of allowance—not to be determined exactly by rule; and let the settlement of tenant right be a matter between landlord and tenant, and not, as is usual, between outgoing and in- coming tenants. Thus it will be seen that the landlord has,l as a matter of fact, the greater part of a year's rent in hand on his estate, in the shape of tenant's outlay, which 111 quite enough,'l think, to settle the question of distraint as to one year or two, which subject has been, I see, discussed in many of the leading Chambers of Agriculture. A special compensation clause, I am of opinion, should be inserted in every agreement (amount to be determined by contracting parties), to provide for and meet any sudden compulsory ejectment caused by estate being ' sold in the event of death and change of proprietorship, 1 as happened in a case I have good reason to remember in 1872, in which year land (agricultural) rose to a higher value than has hitherto been known. A small estate 1 changed hands in consequence of death of owner—a fine old English gentleman. Tenants and their families been occu- piers near to and upwards of a century; holdings varying 1 from 200 to 500 acres each; about six of them, and cot- I tagers. Result was, the sale realised "in lots" about 15e. an acre more than the then tenants thought it worth. One ' farm (300 acres), renting at 30s. an acre, was bought by a I land speculator, and not being able to re-sell, let it on a , seven years' lease at 50s. per acre. The new spirited tenant 1 at end of term did not renew, but said he had got well 1 1 "peppered." You will say, serve him right. But how 1 about the late tenant—home broken up (for farms could not then be had for asking)? Home! The place in which the staff was struck is still known as Beckett's Well; but the peculiar construction of the enclosure which con- tains the water leaves little doubt as to its haying been a Roman bath, which was possibly utilised by the popular saint. Pieces of Roman tile found in its proximity also seem to confirm this supposition. As the water of the well is believed to be a medicinal quality, St. Thomas is said to have bathed in it for the benefit of his health ; and in later time the Archbishops of Canterbury, when worn out with old age or sickness, used to retire to their manor of Otford for the same purpose.—Cassell's Family Magazine.

"In fair Provence—, the latd of lu`e and rose, Arnaut, great ma9ter of the lore of love, First wrought Eestines to win his lady's heart, For she was deaf when simpler staves he sang, And for her sake he broke the bonds of rhyme. And in this subtler measure hid his woe. Harsh be my lines," cried Arnaut, `harsh the woe- 2y[y lady, that enthroned and cruel rose, Indicts on him that made her live in rhyme.' But through the metre spake the voice of Love, And like a wild-wood nightingale he sang, 'Who thought in crabbed lays to ease his heart. "It is not told if her untoward heart Was melted by her poet's lyric woe, Or if in vain so amorously he sang; Perchance through cloud of dark conceits he rose To nobler heights of philosophic love, And crowned his later years with sterner rhyme. "This thing alone we know the triple rhyme Of him who bared his vast and passionate heart To all the Crossing flames of hate and love, Wears in the midst of all its storm of woe As some loud morn of March may bear a rose— The impress of a song that Arnaut sang. " ` Smith of his mother tongue,' the Frenchman sang Of Lancelot and of Galahad, the rhyme That beat so bloodlike at its core of rose, It stirred the sweet Francesca's gentle heart To take that kiss that brought her to flinch woe, And sealed in fire her martyidona of love. "And Dante, full of immortal love, Stayed his drear song, and softly, fondly sang As though his voice broke with that, weight of woe And to this day we think of Arnaut 's rhyme Whenever pity at the labouring heart On fair Francesca's memory drops the rose. "Ah sovereign Love, forgive this weaker rhyme; The men of old who sang were great at heart, Yet have we too known woe, and worn thy rose." From • New Poems," by E. W. Gone. The last words of the lines of each stanza are the same, in a different order.

MRS. GRAMMAR'S BALL. Mrs. Grammar she gave a fine ball To the nine Parts of our speech; To the great and the small, To the short and the tall, There were pies, plums, and puddings for each. And first little Articles came In a hurry to make themselves known; Fat A, An, and The; But none of the three Could stand for a minute alone. Then Adjectives came to announce That their dear friends the Nouns were at hand, Rough, rougher, roughest; Tough, tougher, toughest; Fat, merry, good-natured, and grand. The Nouns were indeed on their way— Tens of thousands and more, I should think. For each name that we utter. Shop, shoulder, or shutter, Is a noun; lady, lion, and link. • The Pronouns were following fast, To push the Nouns out of their places; I, thou, you, and me, We. they, he, and she, With their merry, good-natured old faces. Some cried, "Make way for the Verbs,' A great crowd is coming is; view, To bite and to smite, To light and to fight, And to be and to have and to do. The Adverbs attend on the verbs, Behind them as footmen they run; As thus, to fight badly, Then run away gladly, Shows how fighting and running were done. Prrpositions came, in, by, and near, With Conjunctions, a poor little band, As either you or me. But neither they nor he; And held their great friends by the hand. Then in with a hip! hip! hurrah! Rushed in interjections uproarious, Oh dear! well-a-day ! When they saw the display Ha ha! they all shouted out glorious But alas! what misfortunes were nigh, While the fun and the feasting pleased each, There pounced in at once, A monst-er, a dunce, And c3nfounded the nine Parts of speech Help! friends, to the rescue : on you For aid noun and article call; • Oh: giv,! your protection To poor interjection, Verb, adverb, conjunction and all.

A new Radical Club is about to be formed in Barrow. Barrow has been accepted as a port at which tobacco can be imported. The Glasgow Liberal Association has, through its Chair- man, condemned the Fair Trade agitation. The Pilotboat Hotel at Falmouth was destroyed by fire early on Monday. The damage is covered by insurance. Meetings were field on Monday at Muchalls and Bench- ory, Kincardineshire, at :which resolutions were passed in favour of land reform and substantial diminution of rents. The King of the Sandwich Islands visited Liverpool on Monday, and under the guidance of the Mayor made the customary round of sight-seeing. In the evening his Majesty was entertained at a banquet in the Town-hall. The newly-elected central executive of the National Land League of Great Britain held its first meeting on Tuesday, in Westminister, Mr. Justin M'C'arthy, M.P., presiding, and in accordance with the powers conferred by the conven- tion, 20 additional members were added to complete the body. The proposal to erect a monument in Dumfermline Abbey, to the memory of the late Dean Stanley, is meeting with hearty reception in all parts of the country. Principal Tulloch, of St. Andrew's, has intimated his wittiness to become a member of the committee to carry out such an object. A GHASTLY CARGO.—A sensation has been caused in Bristol by the discovery that a cargo of 300 tons of human bones is now being discharged to the order of a local firm of manure manufacturers. The bones were shipped at Rodosto, and are remains principally of the noble defenders of Plevna. The hair still adheres to some of the skulls, and complete limbs are amongst the horrible contents of the cargo. A shocking affair is reported from Newtown, Ebbw Vale. Late on Saturday night a man named Timothy Dempsey was behaving in a violent manner in the street, when his sister-in-law called out to him through the window to desist. He then rushed into the house, and it is alleged, stabbed her in the arm with a knife. She bled so profusely that death ensued on Sunday. Dempsey is now in custody. Addressing a meeting of his constituents at Dudley, on Monday, Mr. W. H. Gladstone said that a Land Bill would have to be provided for England, and he believed that ere long the people would insist upon an extension of the franchi.e to the counties. In his reference to Irish affairs, Mr. Gladstone said that grievances were Mr. Parnell's stock-in-trade. THE DUKE OF HAMILTON AND HIS ARRAN TENANTRY.— Excitement is daily increasing amongst the tenantry of the Duke of Hamilton in Arran in consequence of changes that are rumoured to be imminent. General meetings have been quietly held by the tenantry, and at a meeting held on Thursday evening it was resolved to unite in some move- ment that would gain them leases of their farms and put an end to the system of tenancy at will. Commenting upon land tenure in Wales, Mr. W. R. H. Powell, M.P., states that he trusts something will be done to stimulate tenants to lay out more money in the cultiva- tion of their farms. Any measure which will give that greater security to tenants which they richly deserve will —.--.. have his hearty support. Writing to a Coventry gentleman en the subject of fair trade, Mr. Bright says: "As to the question of fair trade, I may remark that the fairest—that is, the most free and just —trade is when every man may buy from the person who serves him best, and sell to every man who comes to him in the character of a good customer. For nations the same rule holds. Fair trade for a nation exists when its laws do not interfere with itg freedom and power to purchase and to sell among all other nations. As individuals we are all free traders, and therefore fair traders, and our interests as a peo- ple or a nation invite us to a like policy. If anyone give you other advice, depend upon it he is either ignorant or worse than ignorant. If you apply to the secretary of the Cobden Club you may &stain copies of recent publications of the speeches of Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Cross, which are conclusive with all who can read and understand, and of a good pamphlet by Mr. G. W. Medley, entitled The Reci- procity Craze.' fhese publications give abundant facts and arguments. This 'fair trade' cry is for the most part a scheme on the part of a portion of the Tory party to bring over to them such of our population as have no remembrance of the condition of the country forty years ago, and who are ignorant of the extraordinary advance in wealth which the country has made since free trade became our natioaal policy, and of the great increase of comfort and indepen- dence among the labouring and wages-receiving classes of our people.'

How PRINCESSES DRESS.—Says the London correspondent of the Philadelphia Times :—" I have seen the three little daughters of the Prince and Princess of Wales at the opera with their parents, when, on one occasion, the little one getting sleepy, her mother took her up on her lap and let her sleep there on her knees all the evening; I have seen them at charitable ceremonies which were attended by much pomp and circumstance; I have seen them riding, driving, walking, boating, and on none of these occasions, I venture to say, did the wearing apparel of each one of the little girls exceed in cost a $lO bill. A simple white muslin frock, un- decorated by any lace, unrelieved by any silk slip or expen- sive sash, formed the opera costume. The winter and boat- ing dresses are of serge, the summer dresses of washing prints. And all are made in the simplest style—no goffer- ings, puckerings, flounces; no bias bands, no knife plait. legs. No feathers in the hats; no furbelows anywhere. Would that the Mrs. Lefties' of America, those vulgar and tasteless creatures who are at the present time at the water- ing places all over the country and making the bodies of their children a mere means of parading their power to spend money, and who are ruining the moral health of their offspring by inculcating in these impressionable young breasts a mad passion for personal adornment—would that these silly and reprehensible mothers, I say, could be here to see the pattern set in this matter by the Princess of Wales. The example is followed, as all examples are when coming from the fountain-head of social eminence, and the result is seen in the admirable dressing of young English people, universally extolled in every community of taste." AN IMPERIAL Joxe.—Among many amusing anecdotes of the Russian Imperial family related in the late Karl Bender's Memoirs is the following highly characteristic story of the eccentric Grand Duke Constantine, the late Czar Alexander's eldest uncle. While residing at Warsaw , Constantine gave a splendid banquet to a number of great I Polish nobles, to each of whom, at the conclusion of the feast, an ordinary tallow candle was served on a plate by the attendant lacqueys. As soon as all his guests were supplied with these peculiarly unappetising objects, the Grand Duke, who had given orders that an imitation candle, admirably executed in marchpane, should be placed upon his plate, rose from his seat and exclaimed, "Gentlemen, let us eat to the honour of Russia, the favourite national comestible of my country. Look at me. This is the way to do it." So saying, he threw back his head, opened his mouth wide, and inserted therein two inches cr so of the dainty in question. As he closed his teeth, however, the expression of his coun- tenance suffered an extraordinary change. One of the noblemen sitting in his immediate vicinity had contrived to substitute his own genuine tallow candle for the marchpane imitation set before the Grand Duke, who, not choosing to betray himself to his guests, found himself condemned to chew at least one copious mouthful of good Russian tallow, as an example to all the victims of his detestable jest, none of whom, of course, dared to abstain from doing as the terrible Constantine did. It is needless to say that the dexterous appropriator of the marchpane candle, while de- vouring that toothsome article with a joyful heart, baffled suepcion by the most hideous visual contortions expressive of loathing and nausea.—Home Journal. THE MODERN FRENCHILIN.—The vivacity and politeness of the French of all classes are proverbial, and we blunt and phlegmatic Englishmen might well take a lesson from them. But a larger and closer acquaintance discovers other quali- ties. The modern Gaul, like his supposed ancestors of I Galatia, is a being of strong impulses, easily swayed by his I passions to deeds of generosity or cruelty, and governed by 1 sentiment more than by principle. His feelings are quickly stirred ; but his heart is not as easily moved. The portrait , of his nation was truly drawn in the hearing of the writer, I with a few bold touches, by one peculiarly qualified to form I a judgment and to express it. "The spirit of the French," said M. Loyson, better known as Pere Hyacinthe, "is at once revolutionary and bound by routine" (revoluticranaire et routinier). The remark is paradoxical, but the contra- diction may be curiously traced through both their national and private life. They are not readily induced to turn from the well-worn tracks which custom or tradition has marked out. They love the old paths, and are pre-eminently crea- tures of routine ; and yet, as their eventful history proves, I may be roused to momentary flashes of enthusiasm. Now, this peculiarity of our neighbours is at once a help and a hindrance to efforts for their spiritual good. It renders ; them remarkably open to such efforts. Approach them in a kind and respectful manner, without patronising (for that they at once resent), but as a friend and a brother, with a genuine wish to be of use to them' and you may generally count upon a ready and respectful hearing. The rude re- pulse or scoffing jest, so common amongst the ignorant and godless here, are rarely met with in Paris. And if the speaker have something to say, and know how to say it, he I may insure an attentive and appreciative audience.—The Quiver. A WORD TO CHARITY GIVERS —HOW do We„ SS a matter of fact, act in ordinary matters of charity? We are on a 1 committee to bestow a pension, to elect to an asylum or a ! school. Is there any sense of discharging a trust with I reference to the community at large? Generally we act on the merest personal considerations. We have been asked te give our votes; those who asked us gar- us theirs ii , similar case. The person is a relation, a Cr' - a depand ant. ! The misery of the individual case weigl - upon us. But I surely if the judicial aspect of the duty a before us, we should take a wider outlook. We should consider not so I much the effect of our charity on the individual, but on the community of which he is a member; we should in the highest light think of it as affecting the interests of the kingdom of which both of us are members. If it could be I shown that, warped by partiality, we had passed a sentence which would encourage others in those habits which pro- duce the very misery we are trying to relieve, those habits which are the worst enemies of the community or the king- dom, then we should be seen to be unjust judges, who have been bribed by undue influence to turn away the really I needy from his rights, and to strengthen the bands of the wicked. We cannot see the evil of our conduct except in the light of its effects, and therefore let us ask what must be the effect of the constant creation of large funds to help the families of those who, having been in receipt of wages at which our east-end poor would rejoice, are suddenly de- prived by accident or death of the power of maintaining their belongings? Could any plan better be devised to make them spend freely than the assurance that the sudden- ness of the fate which overtakes them will create such sympathy that their families will be amply provided for? If the funds must be raised, at least let them be distributed In proportion to the insurance the man has effected during his life, and let the man who makes no provision be branded as an enemy to society. In our present way of charity we, In our pity for the special cases, lose sight of the wrong done to the needy whose cases are not made thus promi- nent, who none the less have fought a better fight. And meanwhile we are losing the discipline which comes of wise seltrepression. We are losing that insight into character which the careful consideration of a difficult case entails. We are losing that knowledge of our relation to God, and His relation to us, which in these later days may be thus best studied.—Rev. Brooke Lambert, in Good Words. At a numerously attended meeting of the General Com- mittee of the Farmers' Alliance, on Monday, Mr. James Howard in the chair, a resolution was passed expressing the opinion that any concerted action between the farmers of the kingdom and those manufacturers who are seeking to revive Protection would be most unwise upon the part of the farmers. The committee believed that if it were pos- sible by united effort to reverse the national policy of Free Trade and to restore Protection, the first interest to be sacrificed would be that of agriculture; that if duties upon corn could be reimposed they would be repealed at the first moment of difficulty, and this whichever party happened to be in power. The committee could not, therefore, but look upon the agitation for "Fair Trade" as a delusion and a snare; a delusion because, whilst there is not the remotest chance of the nation listening to any proposal to tax its i food, duties on farm produce, even if allowed, would not only be of no perrhanent benefit to the tenant farmer, but would prove injurious to his interests by raising the price of foreign corn, now so largely required for stock feeding; ' snare, because the proposal is an expedient for keeping up rents, and for staving off agricultural reforms, xrhich are the ' only true remedies in the hands of Parliament for restoring prosperity to the farming interest.

"Nothing on earth, or, for that matter, in heaven," said the questioned one, "but Lowther has as good. an eye for a horse as an ostler or a veterinary surgeon. That's the reason he's sent to Ireland. MYRA'S JOURNAL for September contains a fund of useful and interesting information for ladies, models of the latest costumes, patterns, and well written articles on dress, the cuisine, etiquette, needlework, &c. THE EMIGRANTS FRIEND (Newcastle-on-Tyne: The Tyne Publishing Co.)—We have here a new edition of this guide for emigrants by Major Jones, United States Consul, con- taining a fund of useful and valuable information. The author says his object is not "to encourage emigration to the United States, but rather to furnish complete authentic and impartial information to those who contemplate leaving the 'old home' to try their fortunes in the west." The work contains full information on agriculture, cost of living, wages, &c., with the peculiarities of each State, its products. &c.; the whole of the information being of a decidedly prac- tical character, the study of which by intending emigrants would enable them to avoid many trials.

Messrs. Cassell, Petter, Galpin, and Co. have just issued the first monthly part of " The Peoples of the World," edited by Dr. Robert Brown, profusely illustrated. This is a new edition of the "Races of Mankind" so entirely re- cast and greatly enlarged as to be actually a new book bringing the descriptions abreast of the latest standpoint of knowledge. COMPLETE GUIDE TO TEE HOME CIVIL SERVICE k Lon- don. F. Warne and Co.).—This is an excellent guide for candidates for the civil service, written by Mr. A. C. Ewald, F.S.A., a member of the service. It contains directions for candidates, specimens of recent examination papers, details of salaries, (Szc. This is the 13th edition of this useful work, which has been entirely re-written to include all the recent changes of regulations introduced into the service.

Lieutenant. General Sir Garnet Wolseley says :—The cause of temperance is the cause of social advancement. Temper- ance means lees crime, and more thrift and more of comfort and prosperity for the people. Nearly all the crime in our Army is traced to intoxication and I have always found that when with any army or body of troops in the field there was no issue of spirits, and where their use was prohibited, I the health as well as the conduct of the men were all that could be wished for. There was a parochial school, in a remote muirland dis- trict of a southern Scotch county, at which the attendance had, from various causes, at one time dwindled down to a single self-reliant boy; and one forenoon, in a lull of school work, the little fellow looked up with a reflective air and said, "Meister, I think the schule 'll no be here in the morn." "What puts that in your head, sir?" haughtily inquired the master. To which the callant immediately re- plied, "Because I'll no be here."

EMINENT LAWYERS AS SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS.— Of those in our day who have attained distinction, we may mention the present Lord Chancellor, Lord Se'borne • the late Ch meellor, Earl Cairns; and his predecessor, the late Lord Hatherley. These are all men of unsullied reputation; men of high Christian principle; men whose Christianity has not been confined to mere profession, nor even to a blameless life, but who have given themselves eernestly and humbly to active Christian work in one or more of its various departments. Under the pressure of grave and even tremendous responsibilities, and circumstances of immense difficulty, from which many have fled for relief to scenes of gaity and dissipation, they have bad recourse to the Chris- tian's stronghold of prayer, and have sought relief in gather- ing up the strains of sacred song, or in scattering the seeds of truth in the minds of the young in the Sunday-school, where they have readily taken their place among the rank and file of this noble army of Christian workers.—From ' The Quiver" for September. div.head: LEIGH AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: LEIGH AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

• SIR R. A. CROSS ON FARMERS' PROSPECTS. Ten years ago the Leigh Agricultural Society, whose ex- hibitions had been held annually from its establishment in 1860, found itself through a variety of causes in a condition of collapse, and the yearly show was abandoned. After a decade of desuetude the exhibition has been ievived, and the first meeting of the new series was held on Wednesday under favourable circumstances, especially as regards the weather. I There were about 900 entries, the numbers in the various classes being-horned cattle 19, horses 55, turnouts 9, pigs 25, poultry 100, pigeons 50, dogs 154, butter 12, eggs 14, farm and garden produce 266, extra stock 9, agricultural implements, dm., about 190. The following gentlemen acted as judges: Cattle and implements, Mr. William Boyes, Tawd Side Farm' Latham. Horses, Mr. Wm. M. Graham, Manchester, and Captain Heaton, Worsley. Poultry, Mr. Simon Fielding, Trentham Park. Horticulture, Mr. W. B. Upjohn, Worsley ; Mr. Wm. Baillie, Heaton Park. Dogs, Mr. C. E. Lawson, Park Gate, Rotherham; Mr. R. Alston, Leigh Lodge, Sale; Mr. Win. M. Graham. Pigeons, Mr. S. Wade, Baildon ; Mr. Percy Heaton, Worsley. rigs, Captain Heaton. Farm produce, Mr. Henry Crosby, Sale. . In the afternoon a public luncheon was held in a marquee on the show ground, and was numerously attended. Sir R. A. Cross, M.P. (president of the society), occujoied the chair. The right hon. gentleman was accompanied by Lady Cross, Miss Cross, Colonel Cross, Colonel Ireland Black- burns, M.P., Colonel Sylvester, and Mr. W. B. Hutton ; Sir R. A. Cross and party being at present the guests of Mr. Hutton, at Hutton Park. The toast of "The Leigh Agricultural Society" was pro- posed by Col. BLACIEBURNE, M.P., who in the course of his remarks alluded to the difficulties under which agriculturists had laboured during the last month in regard to the weather. The farmers had persevered in the faced an in- clement season with the utmost bravery, and he hoped they would enjoy the reward they so richly merited in the good time which he believed would come. The interests of land- lords, tenants, and agricultural labourers were *welded to- gether, and this identity of interests must be insisted upon in the future. Any legislation which would have the effect of altering their mutual relations would be a mistake. • , Mr. Mount. Maim acknowledged the toast. Mr. W. JONES proposed The Committee of Manage- ment," coupled with the name of Mr. W. Cuntiffe, the chair- man of the committee, who responded. Mr. RALPH FLETCHER proposed "The health of the President," which was very heartily drunk. The CHAIRMAN, in responding, complimented the farmers of this country on the manner in which had borne the diffi- culties and hardships of the last four or five years. British farmers, he said, were often terrified at the great im- portations from America, and there was no doubt that prices had been depressed at the time their crops had been small, and that as a consequence there had been great suffering; but he believed that in the long run they would win the I day. Whilst the American harvests had increased, there I was no doubt but that the consuming power throughout the world had also increased, and he believed the time would come, and very shortly, too, when we should feel that but for this abundant harvest outpouring we should hardly have known what to do. At the same time the present state .of things pressed very hardly upon us, and it was necessary that landlords, tenants, and labourers should pull unitedly, heart and soul, together. Of late years especially extra burdens had been thrown upon land, and there was need ot relief in that respect. Some relief had already been given, but to his mind not enough, and he hoped the time would speedily come when still further relief should be given to this overburdened interest. Any such proposition, from whatever quarter it emanated, would receive his hearty support. THE EXANIINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 17, 1881 ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL. MISSIONARY MEETING AT ST. HELENS. REV. W. G. PASCOE ON CHRISTIANITY. On Sunday, the Rev. W. R. Bird, of Hull. preached two sermons in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Westfield-street, in aid of the missionary cause. On Monday evening a missionary meeting was held, presided over by the Rev. R. J. Ward (Congregationalist). There were also present Revs. I'. Willshaw (Primitive Methodist), J. Brown (Presbyterian), W. G. Pascoe (Wesleyan), W. C. Tayler (Baptist), and J. Sarvent (United Methodist). After Mr. Wilshaw had read the report, The CHAIRMAN said he was sure they had listened to the report with great interest. He was particularly struck with two things that came up in the work in Africa, namely, that those who had been made to hear the gospel and those who had been brought to accept it, were now helping themselves. They were now becoming more and more self-supporting ; and that was one of the most encouraging features that came before them in missionary work. The churches were be- coming less and less dependent on the parent society ; they were more and more developing their own resources, and were sending help, very much help indeed, over to the parent society. Young native pastors were being raised up to preach the gospel in their own way. Mr. Ward then said —as he had another meeting to attend—he would ask Mr. Wilshaw to release him. The Rev. C. TAYLER then took the chair, and said the report was very encouraging, as it locked forward with cer- tain hope to the future. He liked that, because if they looked forward with certain hope their hands need not hang down and their knees need not be feeble. He then intro- duced The Rev. W. Gr.rvas PA,COE, who said it was always pleasant to him to take part in an evangelical alliance meeting. One of the most remarkable religious councils in the history of the Christian world was taking place. During the past week and during the current week a most remark- able council had met, and was meeting together, because it represented all the religious Christian missionary societies that God had ever brought into being. No Protestant society numbered so many millions of adherents as the churches embraced in the great Methodist Church. He was very glad of the (Ecumenical Conference now being held in the City-road. He must say that the element of hopeful- ness running through the report could also be applied to their common Christianity. He should have very little faith indeed in any society- that was not imbued with the spirit of hope. When a man gave up hope he was done for, and when a church gave up hope its work was done. He was looking forward with great hopefulness to the issue of the Council with regard to the (Ecumenical gathering. They must hope that whatever of division had characterised them would be smoothed away, and whatever was essential to the progress of Christian liberty and harmonious working may be the outcome of that gathering. Christianity gave them a desire to impart to others what they had themselves received ; and when God set a man on fire in love to Him depend upon it no difference of skin, be the men white, black, or red, or whatever might be the facial construction of the individual, the man would tell out the hope that he had received. Ha had no faith in that system of religion which demanded "Thus eaith the Lord " to everything that was done ; he had no faith in that religion which ordered a man to do any work before he dare engage in it. He believed in the impulsion of the grand spirit which led a man to do a grand work whether he was ordered to do it or not, because the burning fire was in him, and must either break out or destroy the whole structure. He remembered Max Muller once said that there were three elements of religion that tend to the one essential element of progression. They were Mahommedanism, Buddhism, and Christianity, and the essential element of progress and continuance was the missionary spirit and the almost prophetic weight to struggle for final prominence amongst the races holding those three great faiths. That was the judgment of an exceeedingly keen mind, a thoughtful man, a great philosopher, and great scholar, and he accepted it as being the judgment that was founded on the principles of truth itself, and was in harmony with every conviction of the oracles of God. The final struggle for prominence would be between those forms that were missionary in char- acter, and he had no doubt as to the outcome; as to the issue. And those words quoted at the conclusion of the re- port would fihd their ample fulfilment in the march of time, —"He must reign." Some people would say that Christianity was eminently suitable for our western modes of life, but whilst ,ve found it suitable it was utterly ridiculous to suppose that Christianity was suitable to everybody. John Stuart Mill had said there were other ethics besides those evolved by Christianity. He (the speaker) wanted to know what moral ethics existed in the minds of the Hottentots, and Bushmen, in the minds of the inhabitants of the Fiji Islands, the New Zealanders, or the Red Indians of North America. They found none. There was no thought of morality, no thought of a moral life. But Christianity had been the parent to beget those very things; and the answer to such objections, and the adaptability of Christianity to all men was—" show us the nation to which Christianity is not adapted; show us the nation in which Christianity has been inoperative, uninfinential ; show us the nation where Christianity has failed to secure dignity; show us a tribe of men that have never been enabled to accept its truths, because of incapacity and unsuitableness." Where were they to be found. Echo answers "Where !" They were not to be found. There was not a spot on the surface of the globe where Christianity was to be found, that had not been blessed bylthe holy word. It left behind a final testi- mony of its adaptability to all races of men. The old Grecian spoke in his poetry of a fair maid passing across a desert, and in whose every footstep flowers sprang up; and that had been verified in their Christianity. Christianity was stepping along the moral waste of this world, and wherever her footsteps rested, a host of good and beautiful things sprang up and adorned the pathways of her ministry. There had never been found a race of men yet, but what Christianity had been able to meet the requirements of that race, elevate its morality, and sanctify its relationships. Others said that Christianity in the past had done a great work; that it took the place of the old philosophies, and removed them out of the way. And as it took away the Judaisms, so it in its turn would be put out of the way by some universal forms of belief, satisfying their loftier instinct and greater demands. They also said there was great hostility manifested on the part of the leaders of thought, who were covertly, if not openly, hostile to Christianity. He (the speaker) had met that argument in the New Testament. He found that the people trumped up that charge so long a time back. Pride of in- tellect might do that. He could understand a man trained in the schools of science asking for a demonstration of every ' problem; and he expected to apply the same thing to Chris- tianity, to apply mathematics to it. But they must not come to Christianity and ask for a mathematical demonstra- tion. Christianity asked them to believe in God, because God had revealed his will that there should be faith, credence, a receptive heart. If a man expected demon- aetrated problems, Christianity had nothing to say to him. Withoet faith it was impossible to please God. Pride of Intellect sometimes kept a man out of the kingdom, whilst a poor humble believer passed in. A philosopher needed con- version as well as a peasant. Call a man what they liked, whether he had a ponnd a week or one hundred, the same pressure must take place in the case of every man. (Cheers.) He was looking forward to the time when there would not be a single department of science but what would bring its incite of influence to bear in favour of Christianity. Mr. Pascoe then related how a minister of the Gospel, whom he knew, after working bard at his manuscript dreamt that he was in a spacious hall, which was divided into sections. In one room there were specimens of rock, fossils, &c., which showed that it was devoted to geology. In another room there were plants of all sorts, and illustrations embellished the walls. In this room people were heard to talk about climate, and its effect upon the plants. In another room there were paintings and sculpture, and people were heard to converse about lines of beauty. In nother sectiop of the hall piles of books were reared, there were innumerable maps on the wall, and people were heard to talk about dynasties and dynastic alliances. This room was devoted to history. In the first room one of the leaders took up a book 1 and read, "He only is my rock and salvation," and in the ' room devoted to botany the leader read, "He is the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valley." In the art room another read out of the book, "lie is the fairest among ten thousand and altogether levely ;" and in that section set apart for history the words read were, " His kingdom is an everlast- ing kingdom, and shall have no end." (Cheers.) He be- lieved that from every quarter of human investigation and intellectual research there would come additional evidence to the truth of their holy faith. (Applause.)

WELCOME TO NEW WESLEYAN MINISTER AT ST. HELENS.

The new superintendent Wesleyan minister has now com- menced his pastorate at St. Helens in the place of the Rev. J. A. B. Harry. On Thursday evening a formal meeting of introduction was held in the Waterloo-street schoolroom. About 40 Sunday school teachers and School Committee assembled together and enjoyed a social cup of tea, and afterwards the formal welcome of the Rev. J. M. Walmsley took place.—After singing and prayer, the Rev. W. G. PASCOE said it fell to his lot to introduce to them one to whom, he was sure, they would giye a hearty welcome. Not one of the least of the signs of prosperity that could attend the operations of any church was a minister who was as one with the office bearers of that church, a sympathy spring- ing from one central bond of union, who were animated by the same great passion, the love of God, and the love of souls. With such conditions the Church of Christ might be wherever planted a glorious success ; but in order to attain that end; one of the most important things was, that, from the chief officer in their midst down to the very lowest worker, there should be a common sympathy and fellow feeling running all the way through, One important thing was to look out for the minister who would occupy the position of the first minister, one who to a very considerable extent could inspire the workers that associated with him during the time that he occupied that position; to look out for one who could have full sympathy with them, and could grasp the hand of a fellow worker wherever he might meet him, and one in whom the whole of the office bearers could feel they were in full sympathy. He had great pleasure in introducing Mr. Wabusley to them. He had not known him long, but be had known him sufficiently long to feel that in grasping his hand he was grasping the hand of a brother, and of a man. He believed he was a man of right judgment, warm sympathy, large heart. (C3heers.)—The Rev. J. M. WALMSLEY, after a few Jocular remarks, tendered his hearty thanks to Mr. Pascoe, and through him to them, for their sincere and cordial greeting, for he regarded everything Mr. Pascoe had let fall from his lips, as having come from the depths of their hearts, and their feelings found an echo in his. He fully endorsed the latter part of Mr. Pascoe's address. The best advice to a preacher was "aim at the fifth button," for there they found the heat. If he could not be warm he could be nothing. He had not graduated in the starch college. (Laughter.) Starch AV3S all right for getting up linen. (Laughter.) A little bit of sunshine was his loftiest conception of the life that now is. There were the shadows; there were the passing clouds that flung their shadows across their path, but still his loftiest conception of life was wrapped up in one word—"sunshine." (Applause.) He believed in a cheerful religion, and by the grace of God he would endeavour to keep ap such a religion. Mr. Pascoe had'said something about the hand, He often admired the hand ; it had a wonderful significance in its grip, apart from the mechanism. The moral significance of it, the intellectual power, and moral sympathy that found expression in that wonderful piece of creative power, skill and genius, had a very great significance. Well, he would try to use his hand. (Cheers.) Some tel ks did not know how to use their hands, hut placed them in somebody else's in a very nauseous fashion, self he anticipated finding something there he did want to touch. He liked the hearty, loving, simple style, and believed in getting hold of the hearts of the children, for if they did that, they got hold of the hearts, the moral, and intellectual forces of this, the next, and all succeeding generations.

div.head: RESPONSIBILITIES OF CHEMICAL MANUFACTURERS.
div.p: THE RESPONSIBILITIES OF CHEMICAL MANUFACTURERS.

The Town Clerk having written, according to instructions, to some of the chemical manufacturers in the town pointing out that acid was found to run from their works into the brook, a letter was read from Messrs. Kurtz stating that in reply to the letter of the Town Clerk, of the 15th inst., they had to express their regret that any cause of complaint as to acidity, however slight, in the drainage from their works into the brook, should have arisen. On making enquiry they found that the escape of weak acid was quite accidental; and, as the town clerk was aware, such an accident was of such rareoccurrence at their works as hardly to warrant the very peremntory tone of the clerk's letter. They were most desirous to comply with the regulations of the Health Com- mittee, and were hopeful of being able to make such further improvements as would make the running of acid water I into the brook, from their works, impossible except in case of accident.—The CHAIRMAN : He generally is very careful, I no doubt.—MEMBERS Oh, yes.—MEnicen OFFICER: I have a reference to it in my report, and I am quite satisfied that they are doing all they can.—A letter was read from the Oreenbank Alkali Works Company in answer to a similar letter. They said that it would appear that, owing to an unfortunate breakage of a pipe, there was an escape of some acid on their works for two days which did not cease all at once, owing to the ground being very porous, being filled up with broken pot pipes. At the same time, they begged to observe that none of the acid would ever have got into the drain if the pipes had been properly puddled, and they hoped that the Corporation in,. relaying the pipes as they were now doing, would so puddle the joints as to make it impossible that any drainage could enter the pipes from the surrounding soil, which was one mass of chemical waste outside their land, and which was placed there long before their time. ' They could, assure the committee that the matter had had their serious attention and they did not think the committee would find any further cause for com- plaint on that subject.J—Messra. Leather, of the Bridgewater Chemical Works, replied that while they much regretted that acid should be found in this liquor flowing from their works into the brook, they thought it most improbable that the acid referred to by the medical officer came from their works, as the whole of their acids'were neutralised; and as they had their drainage tested three times each day, they could speak very positively of its contents, and they had not found any acid in it for a long period. It would materially facilitate the inspection, and the object aimed at by the Health Committee, if the inspector whenever he found traces of acid would at once inform them so that they might investigate the cause, and if needful, remedy it.—The MEDICAL OFFICER said there had been a great improvement at Leather's works. —Mr.Mlsszy said ho believed in what Colonel Gamble said sometime azo that their coning there was useless unless some action was taken; but according to the reports the flow of acid did not appear to be as bad, at present, as pre- viously, and it might not he' wise to do anything decisive that day.—Nothing decisive was done. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The Mratimta OFFICER reported :—Samples of Ecclestou I branch of the brook have been taken by Inspector Williams at the usual places—Spray's bridge, Isridgewater-stseet, by the timber yard, and below Messrs. Daglish's works, and lower down the stream by the Bottle Works. These show, the brook to have been free from acid except On the 22nd August. On that day attention VMS called to a strong smell of sulphuretted hydrogen escaping from an opening of the brook near Boardman's bridge. Some feeble acid coming into the brook from the Bridgewater works drain was evi- dently the cause. This was explained to be the result of accident at the above works. The nuisance was at once abated. Samples taken by Inspector Houghton, from Hard- shaw brook,,at the gas works yard. and other places are free from acid. At the request of Mr. Kurtz's manager, I have been over the works, and inspected the new apparatus for neutralising the weak acid which sometimes escapes from the works; and I am satisfied that Mr. Kurtz will do all that is necessary to keep his drain from conveying a nuisance to the brook. A weak acid is toming from the St. Helens chemical works drain into the Atlas-court sewer. As they are neutralising all the acid, it dust be the Atlas foundry drain which 'contributes this acid, notwithstanding that this drain has been disconnected. This acid has almost dis- appeared when it flows into Oclarook at Warrington New- road. The Rainford brook district has been almost free from acid during the month. Another case of small-pox occurred iat Sutton, n Watery-lane, a month ago. He was removed at once to the Union, and is now convalescent. The house was disinfected, and no new case has been seen. The mortality of the district for the past month has been moderate, being 22.20, against 28.02 in the corresponding month last year. The epidemics of last year at this season were diarrhcea and fever, caused by the heat and dryness that prevailed, a similar state of things was imminent six weeks ago, but the rains of August, though not altogether prevent- ing these epidemics have certainly rendered them more moderate. The weather which had been against the farmers had been for the benefit of St. Helens, evidently. ROUSES UNFIT FOR HUMAN HABITALION. Mr. Hart and the Medical Officer haring certified that three houses in Peasley Cross-lane and two houses in Parr- street were unfit for 'human habitation, and ought to be closed for repairs, an :order to this effect was directed to be served upon Mr. William Kitchen, the owner. THE COST FOR THE PAST YEAR. Mr. HART said that the actual Cost incurred in that department for the past year had been £4,401 16s. Sd., and the receipts for the sale of manure, dzc., realised £l,OOO. His estimate this year was—£4,sss for expenses. and £l,OOO for receipts, being a slight sum in excess of the past year. Of course, the cost of that department must increase every year. This year there would be a slight addition in the cost of provender. THE BATHS. Mr. HART said that last year it was left in his hands to say bow soon it was desirable to let the water run out of the baths. In the winter time they would not have three bathers in the three months, and it was no use wasting the water, because they had to pay for it. He presumed it was their intention to keep the private baths open during the winter.—Mr. %toot ; Oh, yes.—The matter was left in the hands of Mr. Hart. The plunge baths will be closed on Saturday, October listh.—Mr. HART remarked they had had a loss of £5O during the past year. THE SUTTON MANURE DEPGT. A COUPLE SEPARLTED.—Edward Swift, who has for , the last six or seven weeks been residing with his mother in Rigby-street, was charged with assaulting and beating his Wife, who occupies a house in Duke-street—Mr. Swift ap- peared on the part of the complainant, and said the parties had been married about four years. Before marriage each had a family of three children, but there had been no children since. Thq wife's children were all grown up, and able to work, but of the man's children, one of them worked, one formerly did live with the couple, and the third with its grandmother. They had been several times separated. At the time of the alleged occurrence, last Saturday, they were living apart from each other; the man had gone to reside with his mother in ar_other street, leaving the woman and her boys at the house in Duke-street. The man never did provide any of the household furniture. He once provided a certain article, but afterwards took that away. When he married the woman she had a good house of furniture, but he put it up for public auction, and it was bought by the woman's son. So far from providing any furniture for the house, he disposed, as far as he possibly could, of what there was, and got the proceeds of the furniture. On Saturday morning from some indications the woman received she had reason to believe that her husband would be coming to the house to kick up a disturbance; and in order to avoid any disturbance she went out. In about half an hour the woman ascertained that her husband had gone to the house, and she went to see what he was doing. She then saw him climbing up to get through the window, and subsequently heard something being smashed in the house. She got into the house, found that some things had been broken, and that her husband in his dirty clothes had laid down in the clean bed. The man was drunk at the time, although it was in the fore- noon. When the wife went into house he raised up his hand to strike her. He afterwards struck her in the mouth, causing blood to flow; then he threatened to knock her head off. At the time defendant's mother and complain- ant's son entered the house, and as soon as the man saw the son—John Hatton—he flew at him and kicked him several times. There was no doubt that, if it had not been for a neighbotr, either the woman or her son John would have been seriously injured. The neighbour in question, how- ever, took John Hatton away, and prevented his being further abused. Defendant and his mother then quietly made their way towards the door, but the defendant returned, took up an iron shovel, the handle of which was iron as well, and deliberately struck his wife a plow on the right temple. The woman was knocked down by the force of the blow, and her temple severely cut. For a few minutes she lay unconscious on the ground, and some of the bystanders thought she was dead. Of course nobody would suppose for a moment that any wrong would be done to either of them if they were judicially separated. They had been separated voluntarily many times—voluntarily on the part of one; perhaps necessarily on the part of the other. If their worships thought—as he submitted they might pro- perly think—that there had been an aggravated assault com- mitted in that case, then, in addition to any punishmsnt which their worships might think right to impose upon the defendant, they had power—if they chose to exercise it, and if they thought that the life of the woman was in danger, should she continue to live with him—they bad the power to decree a judicial separation, and he should ask them to do that. It was no doubt a beneficent provision of the legislature, introduced within a few years past ; it had been beneficially exercised in various courts, and had been in several cases exercised there. There would be no need to make any provision about the custody of children, because there was no children of the marriage. It would not be necessary to make any provision for the maintenance of the wife, because she had had to live without her husband's help, and she would be no worse off without him. She did not requite his help, and did not ask for any maintenance. Re submitted that the assault was an aggravated one; although their worships could make an order of separation, even if they only imposed a fine for a common assault.—Complainant then went into the box, and gave evidence and her statement was partially corroborated by her son.—Colonel Gamble asked the defendant if he was aware of the consequences which might follow tfleir inflict- ing a penalty upon him for assaulting his wife, and if he wanted a remand.—Defendant asked for an adjournment for sixteen days.—The Magistrates, however, allowed the case to go on, and defendant cross-examined his wife. She denied that she abused his children, or that she at any time put her finger nails through the ear of his little boy. His children were bad, and that injury to the ear had been done ins quarrel with a boy in the street.—Defendant insinuated that he had given her money while they had been separated from each other, but complainant denied this.— The Bench considered the case proved, and fined the defen- dant 10s. and costs. The fine would have been much heavier if the question of a separation had not arisen. They did not wish to make the court into a place for the bringing about of separations, but there appeared to be ground tor a separation in the present case, and they granted an order .for I a judicial separation. •

div.head: MoNDAY.—Before Major Pilkington, and Dr. Twyford. _
div.p: MoNDAY.—Before Major Pilkington, and Dr. Twyford. _

THE WHEEL or FORTS:RTE.—Leonard Harris, a young man, was charged with playing a game of chance in a public place at St. Helens, on Saturday night.—P.C. Cottam said he apprehended the prisoner who was playing at a game called the "Wheel of fortune," on the Fair Ground.. The wheel was divided into eight divisions, one of which bore a penny, so that the prisoner had eleven chances to his op- ponent one. On being searched, the prisoner had 19s. 11frd. in his possession, Pe 11d. of which was in copper.—lle was fined 10s. and costs.

CHARGES AGAINST ENGINEER VOLUNTEERS. - Patrick Gorman was charged with neglecting to pay 118. to the 2nd Lancashire Engineer Volunteers.— Sergeant Major Burns said the defendant was sworn a member of the corps on the sth March, 1875, and he had to pay a subscription at Is. a month. They could not recover more than twelve month's subscriptions. If the defendant had attended a single drill no money would have been required of him. He was not an "efficient," therefore he was liable to pay the amount. If a man would not attend to drill the corps would lose the capitation grant of 30.3.—Defendant was ordered to pay us. and costs.—John Foster. Ezekiel Shannon, Patrick Mur- phy, and Thomas Holcroft were ordered to pay simil amounts with costa—William Thelwell, of Rainhill, was summonedlfor neglecting to pay £2 2s.—Sergt. Major Barns said the defendant was a sapper, and WAS not efficient the whole of last year, and the colonel had lost the capitation grant and 12s. subscription. The defendant was sworn in as a member of the corps in 1876.—1 n cross-examination by Mr. Swift, who appeared for the defendant, witness said that , up to two years ago, the Rainhill members were drilled at that place, but being desired by the colonel to come to St. , Helens, many of the Rainhill people resigned. He believed the defendant sent in his resignation.—Mr. Swift: Don't ' you remember about two years ago the defendant coming to the Volunteer Hall one September night with his clothing to give it up 7—Sergeant Major Burns: No.—Don't you re- member your wife speaking to him F--Sergeant Major Burns: No.—Mr. Swift: Did you not hear that he had been with his clothing ?—Sergeant Major Burns : I heard from Sergeant Goss that lie had been with his clothes.—Sergeant Goss was then called.—Mr. Swift: You know of this, don't you ? Sergeant Goss : I don't sir; I only know that he came in with his clothes, but I had nothing to do with them, and the sergeant-major was not in.—Mr. Swift: And what did you do ?---Szrgeant Goss: I refused his clothes, because the hall was locked up, and I have orders to have nothing to do with them. I don't know that he saw Sergeant-Major Burns' wife.—Mr. Swift: Last sum- mer did you not say to defendant, "Bill, you bad better put your drills in, and then you can get out, because if you don't they will be able to summon you7”—Sergeant. Goes: Yes.—Mr. Swift: Did he not tell you he would not put any more drills in, because he had given his notice 7—Sergeant Goes: Yes.—Mr. Swift: And you admitted that he sent his notice in 7—Sergeant Goes: I admit that he told me SO.— Mr. Swift, in defence, said the defendant joined the corps at Rainhill in 1876, and for three years, down to October, 1879, he rendered himself efficient, and complied with all the rules of the corps. In the year 1879 the authorities— the colonel, he supposed—altered the place of drill. The men at Rainhill had been drilled at Rainhill, where they lived, where they enlisted, and where they expected to be drilled. A number of the members did not wish to do that, and preferred to give their notice and leave the corps, as they were entitled to do. The defendant gave fourteen days notice, which expired on a Friday, and he went with his clothing and appointments to the ball, and saw Sergt. Major Burns' wife and Sergeant Goss. Defendant bad the clothes now, because they were not received at the hall, and he had no wish to keep them. Defendant had done all that he could. A tender of the clothes was equivalent, in point of law, to a delivery. He could not possibly do more, and was entitled to leave the corps.—The magistrates made no order.

I DRUNKENNESS AT THE RED CAT.—Jblin Peet was ed with supplying drink to drunken men, and also wilt permitting drunkenness. Janis Sumner, William Grimaliaw, and George Glover, of ghinford, were sum- moned for being drunk on licensed premises.—P.C. Duerden said that on the 3rd inst., at 9-5 p.m., he was on duty at ,Red Cat village, Rainford, when be heard a great disturb- ance in the Red Cat public-bouse, occupied by John Peet. Most of the company were on their feet; all' appeared to be in drink, and the house was in a perfect uproar. The land- lord *as giving out beer; one glass he served upon Samuel Whittaker, who paid for it. Sumner, who was drunk, got up, went into the back kitchen, and the landlord followed him in. He there saw the landlord serve Sumner with a glass of beer, and &limner paid for it. Sumner staggered about, and spilled his beer on the ground. One of the com- pany took Sumner by the arm, and said the " bobby " was coming; and Sumner, in reply, said that if there was a man as good as himself, let him stand forward. He (witness) then drew the landlord's attention to the condition of Sum- ' ner ; and the landlord said, "Yes, I know he is drunk; I only intended filling him one glass." He told the landlord I he could not let the matter drop, and subsequently he re- ported the matter to the sergeant. In consequence of what the sergeant said to him he again visited the place at five minutes to eleven, and saw Grimshaw, who was drunk, capering about, and trying to amuse the company. ,The landlord was trying to keep Grimshaw quiet. He (witness) then went into the back kitchen, and saw another man named John Glover who was drunk. He drew the landlord's attention to him, and the landlord told , Glover to leave the place. The man staggered into the hick yard, and was making his way into a pig-stye. Witness asked him where he was going, and Glover answered that he I was going home. (Laughter.) Glover on being requested i left the premises and went towards k barn, whet he had been in the habit of sleeping.—Charles Barnes, apprentice joiner, living at Rainford, said there was a raffle for a bicycle
./el:,rOrk„

going on at the public-house, and the winner had to spend 2s. 6d in beer for the benefit of the company. There were about one hundred people interested in the raffle but they were not all there. He should say that Sumner was drunk, but he did not think that Grimshaw was.—Mr. Swift appeared for the defendants, and said their defetce WWI that the men were not drunk. If they had made a mistake they were liable to suffer for it, but it certainly did seem to be a very extraordinary thing that a policeman should have so very low an idea of his own case that he should go about to a number of people—to several people to use the police- man's own words in cross-examination—to get them to coins up for witnesses. But he had only succeeded in getting one.—John Peet said he had kept the Red Cat beerhonse for seven years, and had always kept it respectably and orderly. He denied that the men were drunk; and Grimshaw was only merry."—Morris, Grimshaw, and Glover denied that they were drunk.—The magistrates had no doubt that a great deal of drunkenness was going on, on the night in question, but as the officer was practically uncorroborated they felt they must dismiss the cases. THEFT OF Boors.—Sarah Morris (40), described as a resident of Morpns, was charged with stealing a pair of boots from the shop of Elizabeth Brockbank, Liverpool-rd., St. Helens.—Prosecutrix said that on the Bth instant priso- ner entered her shop and asked for a pair of cheap strong boots. Witness was obliged to leave her to someone else in the shop, as another customer wanted attending to.—Eliza- both Brockbank, jam., said she showed the prisoner four pairs of boots. Ultimately she left 2s. on a pair of boots which she did not take out of the shop, and was to call again in the afternoon. After the prisoner had left a pair of boots were missing.—Prosecutrix said she had some difficulty in getting the prisoner, who complained of headache, out of the shop. She afterwards saw the prisoner with the boots pro- duced on her feet. They were her property.—Prisoner at first denied the charge, then pleaded guilty, and was sent to prison for fourteen days.

TCTESDAY.—Before Mr. Thomas Pilkington. A THIEF CAUGHT IN AN OUTBUILDING.—John White, of Sutton, was charged with stealing a coat and vest from the Elton Head Farm, Sutton, the property at Edwsrd Walsh, a farm labourer, and worth £2.—Prosecutor deposed to the property produced being his.—Michael Pigott, a farm labourer, said that at half-past four on the previous after- noon he went into an out-building on the farm, and whilst in the building he heard a noise upstairs. He went up, and found the prisoner there with the clothes produced underneath his own coat, wearing them.—Remanded until Friday.

I HER 37TH APPEARINCE.—Mary Powell made her 37th I appearance, and was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' im- prisonment, for being drunk and disorderly in Tontine- street, at a quarter-past twelve that (Tuesday) morning. It was stated that Mary had served six months for assaulting the police, and had only just come out of gaol. ROBBING A FELLOW LODGER.—John Mackey, about 30 years of age, was charged with stealing, some time betweea Saturday gternoon and Monday morning, £5 in gold from a house in Sutton, the property of Joseph Malone, a fellow lodger.—Prosecutor said he left his box, which contained the money, safe in his bedroom on Friday, and the key of the box was in his waistcoat hung up in the room. He lived at 3, Back Sutton-road, Sutton.—P.C. Carter said that at ten minutes past five on Monday afternoon he apprehended the prisoner in the Robin Rood beer-house, Tontine-street, and on searching biro found in his possession £4 14s. Id. He charged the prisoner with stealing the money, and prisoner replied, "Yes." On putting him into the cell prisoner said, 'I took it because I had no rooney."—Remanded until Friday.

div.head: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT ST. HELENS.

The annual inspection of the 21st L.R.V. was made on Saturday, by CoL H. de R. Pigott, of Warrington, command.. big the Bth and 40th regimental districts. The Colonel arrived at St. Helens at twenty minutes past eleven, and he, accompanied by Lieut.-Col. Gamble, the commanding officer, • and Major and Adjutant Willcocks, proceeded to the Volun- teer Hall, where a close inspection of the buildings, books, the parade ground, and the armoury was made. The Colonel expressed his opinion on what he saw at the Hall at the close of the inspection, as will be seen below. At half-past two o'clock the volunteertmustered at the Hall, from which place they marched to Mrs. Littler's field at Denton's Green, where She anneal inspections for seine time have been held. A goodly number of townspeople visited the field and wit- nessed the variety of movements through which the bat- talion were put in the presence of the inspecting officer. The afternoon was fine. After columns had been formed, they were wheeled into line, took open order and received the inspecting officer, who walked through the rank. The march past then took place, and a number of manual and firing exercises were gone through. A novel feature in the afternoon's movements was the attack upon an imaginary enemy in the cemetery grounds, considerable interest being manifested in this plirt of the proceedings. The inspection over, the Inspecting Officer addressed, the men, and said he had not been able to come amongst them before, and he was very sorry he was unable to accompany them to Windsor at the grand review before Her Majesty the Queen. He had been putting them through the latter part of the drill simply as practice, and did not look upon it gs part of his inspection, but preferred doing it quietly as a drill practice. This was done to show them what was absolutely necessary, and it was an endeavour to instil into their minds the reason for every movement showing that nothing was done but that there was a reason for doing it. The only means to attack and reach the position of an enemy, and do it in the least possible time, and with the smallest amount of loss, was to expose themselves as little as they could to the enemy, and do it quickly; becaase at the best a very large loss must occur in facing an enemy armed with the rifles of the present day, which were made very perfectly, and in accordance with improved knowledge, and in accordance with science. He was most anxious to see them well drilled in attacking a supposed enemy, apd General Cameron, who held the same views, had particularly spoken to him about it. He was sorry to have to correct them for the great amount of talk- ing in the ranks, because with it they could not very effec- tively perform their drill. He was, however, very pleased. with some portions of their movements; the forming of line was very good, and the marching past very fair. He was addressing a regiment that he knew was one of the best. brigades that appeared before the Queen at Windsor a short time ago. He would have been glad and proud to have accompanied them, but he bad to make an inspection the same day, which prevented him carrying out his wishes. The 21st was specially marked for praise, and held up as a pattern by the press. He considered the let and sth corps were a perfect pattern to be copied by the volunteers of the kingdom. He complimented them upon their good shoot- ing. He had inspected the books, and found that the scores were generally very good. They did not appear to have fired the 00 rounds for the sake of making efficient and pass- ing into the body of efficients, but they did it for the love of it. They had apparently paid attention to the snapping and the firing, without which they could never make themselves good shots, if they fired a thousand times a day. He was pleased they had paid good attention to the rules. Colonel Pigott, in conclusion, said he should be able to make a very fair report of the regiment, and so long as he held his present position he should consider it his 'duty and pleasure to do anything he could to improve their drill, and their position as soldiers.—Major Cross, of Widnes, addressed the men, and said they had got a capital report, except for their talk- lug. He hoped they would, take the hint, as he had not heard them talk so much for a long time. In the ground Lbehind the Volunteer Hall before the men had been marched to the field at Denton's Green, an accident occurred to Colonel Gamble. Whilst conversing, on horse- back. with-two officers of the regiment, the colonel's horse reared and threw the colonel heavily to the ground. He at once rose to his feet and mounted the spirited horse, and marched with the men to the field at Denton's Green. Several times during the afternoon the colonel was noticed to exhibit signs of pain while in the saddle, aud frequently placed his hand to his side. The surgeons of the regiment —Drs. WlNTicol and Gaskell—who were not on parade when the mishap took place, arrived on the field in the course of the afternoon, and after watching the colonel spoke to him; and at the close of the inspection accompanied him to his residence at Windiehurst. It was there found that the acci- dent was of more importance than the colonel apparently attached tp it, my of the ribs being slightly fractured, but nothing more serious. The colonel kept his house for? few days afterwards to gain rest, and was attended by Dr. rwy- ford. He is now recovering.

div.head: TRADE I\OTES.
div.p: TRADE I\OTES.
The cotton trade having been so long depressed, a large spinning mill in the East-end of Glasgow is about to close for a time, and a number of card-room bands have already been dismissed.

On Tuesday, about 200 miners, employed in the 7-foot mine of Priestnees pit of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, Westleigh, came out on strike against a pro- posed reduction of 63 per yard, the present rates being 3s 7d and 3s 4d.

A considerable stimulus has been given to the slate trade at Portmadoc lately by an unwonted demand for all kinds of data. Consequently, all vessels arriving at the port are at once chartered. This has naturally caused the wages of the seamen to rise. A.B.'s being offered £3 103. Although this is 80, there is great scarcity of seamen just now, and captains are to b 3 seen everywhere in the neighbourhood looking out for seamen, and thb crews of newly-arrived vessels are immediately shipped.

ALARMING FIRE rrr A WELSH COAL MINE.—A fire broke out on Wednesday in the Pentre Colliery, Ystrad, Glam- organshire, and it was feared the 'lives of a large number of men who were down the pit bad been mall-Iced. Great alarm seems to have been felt for a time as to their safety, fOr large masses of colliers and many women crowd- ed to the mouth of the pit, anxious to ascertain the fate of their relatives and friends. Much excitement prevailed, and as a precautionary measure, the county police at Pontypridd were sent for to keep the mouth of the pit clear; the medical men residing in the locality also repaired there as soon as they heard what had occurred. 'The fire broke out in the engine shed of the pit, and, it was supposed it would have the effect of preventing ventilation. Fortunately all apprehension as to the safety of the men in the pit hark been removed, kr later intelligence has been received to see, effect that they have all been got out of the pjt.;ag- gott ' the fire is being subdued.

Valuable LEASEHOLD PROPERTY, LAwarm), and WAR- RINGTON.—To be SOLD BY AUCTION, by MR. THOMAS SUTTON, on WEDNESDAY, the 21st day of SEPTEMBER, 1881, at 4 for 5 o'clock in the After- noon, at the BLUE BELL INN, HORSEMARKET-STREET, WAR- RINGTON, subject to certain conditions then and there to be produced : LOT I.—All that Valuable Leasehold SHOP and DWEL- LING-110USE, situate opposite to "The Cheshire Chasse," in Latchford, and now in the occupation of Mr. Thomas Norman, joiner, with the outbuildings, workshop, and garden thereto belonging The House contains on the ground floor: Shop, par- lour, kitchen, and scullery; and on the Ist floor three bed- rooms. There is a large enclosed yard at the back of the premises. The Workshop, a large and substantial building, is situate at the rear of the premises and is now used as a joiner's workshop. The let contains 468 1-9th square yards or thereabouts, and has a frontage to Knutsford-road of 36 feet or thereabouts, and is held for the residue of a term of 984 years, from the 25th day of March, 1879, siabject to the yearly ground rent of t 4 17s. 6d. These premises are entirely new, and are well and substantially built, and excellently adapted for business pur- poses. To anyone desirous of commencing in the provision trade or about to establish a milk-selling business, a cc al depot, or any similar business, an opportunity is offered rarely to be met with. LOT 2.—A1l those two leasehold semi-detached VILLAS, situate and being Nos. 5 and 7, in Museum-street, Warrington, with the yards, gardens, and outbuildings belonging thereto, and now or lately in the respective occupations of Messrs. G-. Y. Bolton and J. R Tomlinson. These villas each contain on the ground floor, entrance hall, two large entertaining rooms, kitchen, scullery, and larder. On the first floor there are 5 good bedrooms, w c., lavatory and bath, and in the basement 0 capital cellars. This lot contains (including one halt of and to the centre of Museum-street, and co-exten- sive therewith) 491 superficial square yards of land or there- abouts, and is held for the residue of a term of 995 years frem the 25th day of March, 1878, subject to the yearly ground rent of £l2. The houses are new, and substantially built and heau- tifully finished and decorated, and situated in the pleasantest and most fashionable part of Warrington, and as they will always command a good rent and readily let, this would prove a sound investment. •LOT 3.—A1l tbat Valuable and Commodious SHOP, situate and being No. 79, in Bridge-street, Warrington, and formerly in the occupation of Mr. Richard Dowd, saddler; together with the house, yard, and outbuildings belonging thereto and con- taining on the ground floor Shop (34 feet by 17 feet), sitting room, kitchen, pantry, scullery, and wash-house; on the first floor a large dining-room and 5 bedrooms, and on the second floor 4 bedrooms and a workroom. The shop, dwelling-house, yard. and outbuildings occupy an area of (including one-half of Rose and Crown-street, so far as the same is co-extensive there- with) 348 square yards or thereabouts. Also all those five Cottages, situate and being Nos. 4,6, 8, 10, and 12, in Rose and Crown-street, off Bridge-street, aforesaid, and now in the respective occupations of Esther Taylor, W. Naughton, W. Caldwell, and others; and also all that Smithy and the stables adjoining. The site of the cottages, smithy, and stables (in- cluding one-half of Rose and Crown-street, so far as the same is co-extensive therewith) contains by achneasurement 398 square yards or thereabouts. The whole premises are held for the residue of a term of 999 years, commencing from the 24th day of December, 1840, subject to a chief rent of .E 9 14s. The Shop is ' large and commodious and has a frontage of 20 feet to Bridge- street, which is the buriest thoroughfare of Warrington, and is the principal erArance into the town from Cheshire. The tenant's fixtures to be taken by the purchaser at the valuation of the Auctioneer. The Smithy is now in the occupation of Mr. Hewitt, and a good business is being carried on thereat. The Stables are well built and have accomodation for six horses, and are now in the occupation of Mr. Broadhurst as tenant thereof. For further particulars as to Lot 1, apply to Messrs. JOSEPH DAVIES, VOISEY & DAVIES., Bewsey Chambers, Warrington as . to Lot 3. to Mr, HENRY THORNTON, Insurance Buildings, Mill- street ; and as to all the lots, to the AUCTIONER, at his Office, , in Bewsey-street, or to PERCY DAVIES, Solinitor, 1, Market Place, Warrington.
By Messrs. WILLIAM WILSON 4. _SON.
