I It is the terms upon which he holds his farm which I expose him to the most grievous wrongs. Until those conditions are fundamentally altered, the tenant farmer can never be secure, contented, or permanently prosperous. The wretched harvest weather of several recent summers has immensely aggravated the ill- effects of defective and obsolete land laws. The mass of the farmers in many counties have been reduced to the humiliating state of men who cannot pay the rents they had contracted to pay. Remissions of' liberal percentages of rents on many greatestates have barely enabled the tenants to stay upon their farms, but such allowances came from the landlords in the shape of mere charity, the necessity to crave for which must be humiliating to many a high-minded tenant who has prided himself before time on his ability to pay every man his due. This year, in the midst of their own afflictions, which the Legislature has till now done so little to remove, the tenant farmers of England and Scotland have watched the passage through Parliament of a Land Bill for Ireland of the boldest character. They feel that Irish tenants need the protection of such a measure little more than English, Welsh, and Scotch tenants need it. A Liberal Government and Parliament have done great things for the Irish agriculturists. Farmers on this side are not jealous or resentful because the Irish farmers have had the first turn of the attention of Parliament. But we may be sure that they will not now sit down in indifference if nothing in the same direction is proposed to be done for them. It is not contemplated by It. formers, nor do we believe it is expected by farmers, that a Land Bill as sweeping as that which has been given to Ireland will be enacted for the rest of the United Kingdom. They will ask, indeed, for a Bill on much the same lines as regards the guarantees to them of fair compensation for unexhausted improve- ments on the surrender of their holdings. What other changes of moment tite next Land Act for England and Scotland will embody, we will not attempt to fore- stall. Enough to say that the measure will have to be of different scope and proportions from the Agricul- tural Holdings' Act of the late Government. The struggle to carry a measure algal to the necessities of the case will be severe ; and we cannot tell whether Mr. Gladstone will be prepared to undertake so exact- ing a task so early as the next session, after his tre- mendous expenditure of strength in passing the Irish Act this year. But either next year or the year following, all being well, the Government will no doubt address itself to this great problem in earnest; and it is not too much to ask that the farmers should do all they can to fortify the Government for that undertaking by supporting Liberal candidates at con- tested county elections in the interval.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

I understand that a movement is in contemplation among the Runcorn Friendly Societies to present Canon Barclay with a testimonial of some description, appreciative of the services rendered by him at the Public Hall several weeks ago, when his eloquent words were INtened to by a large and attentive audience, chiefly composed of members of the following clubs: Oddfellows, Shepherds, and Ancient Order of Foresters. The Parish Church, I understand, was placed at the disposal of the members, but it was subsequently arranged they should meet annually in the Public Hall, where everyone would feel at home, irrespective of creed. Last week the annual excursion in connection with the Runcorn Parish Church took place, by steamer, to Liver- pool and New Brighton. Your readers will be pleased to hear that the adult members of the choir, to the number of 14. or 15, were presented with an invitation by ticket to dinner (together with the churchwardens of the Parish Church and the lay readers and choristers of New Town mission school) at the New Brighton Hotel, but only six availed themselves of this opportunity. This NM probably on account of Thursday being the day appointed for the Prince of Wales' visit to Liverpool where many of them went and enjoyed themselves.

By-the-bye, it seems singular that the lay readers of the Parish Church were not invited to dinner. What have they done that they should not have been invited to partake of the good things? An instance of the small value that some people set upon infant life has just occurred this week, at Prescot, and for the sake of our common humanity it is to be hoped that such instances are very rare. At an inquest, held on Wed- nesday, at Prescot, on the body of an infant three days old, it was stated that the decegsed was found in a fit on Tues- day morning, when two neighbours were called in to see it, and, although the mother, grandmother, a lodger, and these two other women were present, the child was left to die without the slightest attempt being made to save its life by sending for a medical man. How mothers of children could passively sit and watch a poor little infant struggling in the throes of death without attempting in any way what- ever to preserve it, I cannot conceive, and the coroner is to be commended for having reprimanded such heartless women. Shakespere says there is "no beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity." Yet here we have a number of women so utterly devoid of it as to leave a poor helpless babe to die before their eyes without endeavouring to assist it. One of them, when asked why she did not send for a doctor, replied, "It had nothing' to do with us," whilst another admitted that she did nothing so long as the child was in the fit, but when she saw it was dead, said, "Send for the doctor." Well might the coroner say that "it seemed strange to him that rational beings—women who had children of their own—could ' see a child in a fit and let it die without making any attempt to save it." Such callous- ness is utterly incomprehensible, and I sincerely hope that the rebuke which these people received in the coroner's court will teach them to show a little of the "milk of human kindness " to helpless babes, when in pain and on the borders of death, in future.

The Assessment Committee of the Runcorn Board of Guardians are making things rather lively in the district. They have given notice that the assessment of the Runcorn, Halton, and Weston Waterworks' Company will be raised from £275 to £l,OOO. The directors may congratulate them- selves upon the fact that they were not able to declare a dividend of five per cent this half year, or the assessment would probably, have gone up to £1,500. It is said that the Gas Company's assessment will also be at once raised.

It is characteristic of the present age that small men are frequently found seeking notoriety by attacking great public then, and I was therefore not surprised to hear that a War- rington Conservative who was present at the Farnworth Agricultural Show had been sneering at Mr. John Bright's explanation of the depressed state of the country being attributable to want of sunshine, and hinting that Mr. Bright a few years ago gave a different explanation of the dulness of trade. I think the public will require better evidence than this gentleman's mere assertion before they will believe in the inconsistency of Honest John Bright, in the face of the unstained and consistent public life he has lived amongst us for above a quarter of a century. The public of Runcorn will be glad to hear that there is a very good prospect of the Waterloo bridge being improved within a brief space of time. The shocking state of the bridge in wet weather, owing to its state of repair, has been the subject of much discussion in the past, but any proposi- tion to del with the matter has formerly been shelved owing to a belief that the Bridgewater Navigation Company were legally bound to repair it. The agreement entered into on the bridge being taken over by the Board has been examined, and it appeared from it that the Board of Commissioners undertook at that time to do the repairs. We understand that the work will be at once proceeded with. FLACCUS.

RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday at the cemetery offices. Mr. Coleburn presided, and there were also present Messrs. Handley, Nor- man, Littler, Moss, Briscoe, and Salkeld (secretary). A statement was read by Mr. Salkeld showing that the inter- ments for the month ending the 25th ult. numbered 19. of whom 10 were Churchmen 7 Dissenters, and 2 Roman Catholics. The deaths in th'e corresponding period of last year were 33. The interments for the five months ending August 25 were 110, and the receipts £lO5 19s 4d, against 122 interments and £99 2s 4d receipts for the corresponding period in the last 12 months. The total number of inter- ments since the opening of the cemetery, up to August 25, had been 5,520, of whom 2,247 Weree-Churchmen 2,818 Dissenters, and 455 Roman Catholics. The Chairman said that the returns showed a total decrease of 29 in the months of July and August, as compared with that period in the previous year. The death rate of Runcorn was at present remarkably low. (Hear, hear.) Mr. James Kirkham sent in a bill of £8 14s for work done at the cemetery mortuary in providing additional ventilation.—Mr. Nornaan :£8 14s •it is tremendous, there is no mistake about it. I think it is too bad for Mr. Kirkham or anyone else to charge the Board at that rate. Mr. Briscoe and Mr. Moss considered the charge far too much.—The Secretary remarked that Mr. Barker, surveyor, had sanctioned the work, which was done in a first-class, workman-like manner. He considered it worth the money charged, and he believed the members would say they were of the same opinion after they had in- spected it. After a little further conversation it was resolved OR the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Norman, that the bill, being an expenditure on capital account, I should be paid out of the sinking fund. Mr. Salkeld stated that the estimated sum required by the overseers for the next six months would be £220. Mr. Handley said that £lOO had been received from the overseers during the month land paid into the bank.—The other business was not of public interest.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER l7, 1881. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER l7, 1881. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

WIDNES OAKLAND -STREET WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—Ort Sunday, two sermons were preached at this chapel by the Rev. J. H. Cummings on behalf of the trust fund. The, Toronto Telegram says: Mr. Thomas Kirkham, a chemical engineer, of Runcorn, Eng., has made an engage- ment with a Liverpool firm to erect soda works in Canada. It is believed that Toronto will be the site selected. DRUNKENNESS IN CHESMBE.—Major ilammersley, Chief Constable of Cheshire, in an order just issued, calls attention to the amount of drunkenness existing in the force, and instructs the superintendents of the division to impress upon constables that drunkenness will not be tolerated; it can only bring discredit on the force, and ruin and disgrace to themselves.. 1 TEMPERANCE AND TIIE.. RUNCORN MERSEY MISSION. —On Monday evening, Mr. Thomas Cooke presided at the I first meeting of the season in connection with the Runcorn Mersey Missions to. Seamen's Band of Hope, which took place at the room, Bottom Locks. The programme consisted of songs and recitations. PROPOSAL TO HOLD THE CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY'S SHOW AT RIINCORN.—The Chairman of the Board of Commissioners, Dr. Steele, has called a public meeting of the inhabitants of Runcorn and district to con- sider the desirability of inviting the Cheshire Agricultural Society to hold its next annual show at Runcorn. The meeting will be held at the Commissioners' Boardroom on Monday next. Mn. BARGER AT RUNCORN.—Mr. T. Barger, who is rapidly taking a first rank as a ventriloquial and musical entertainer, will visit Runcorn Public Hall on Tuesday evening next. We have previously had to speak in the highest terms of Mr. Barger's performances, and we can confidently recommend him to.the notice of the public of Runcorn.

RuNcouN: Mu. A. T. NOWELL'S PICTURES.—We have again pleasure in obserCing that two of the pictures now hanging in the Walker Art Gallery Exhibition, ate drawn by Mr. A. T. Nowell, of Runcorn. The first is an oil paint- ing entitled, "View at Overton." The view is from the hills above the church looking across the marshes to the Mersey. The other picture—a water colour—is " Helsby Hill." Mr. Nowell has also his very excellent water- colour, "Quiet Pleasures," hung at the Manchester exhi- Wtion, it having been previously shown at the Royal Academy. Another picture—an oil painting—entitled, "Still Waters," which is on view at Beaconsfield, Higher Run- corn, is also being shown at Manchester. Mr. Nowell recently received a prize from the National Exhibition at Kensington, which makes the fourth which has been awarded him from the same source.

ROYAL ARCH MASONRY IN CHESHIRE : MEETING or BRIDGEWATER CHAPTER AT RIINCORN.—On Tuesday, the Installation of Principals Elect of *he Bridgewater Chap- ter of Royal Holy Arch Masonry, No. 758, took place at the Misonic Hall, Runcorn. The duties of installing Principal were performed by Companion Stephenson, P.M.E.Z., of Zion Chapter, No. 537, in a most able and impressive manner. The chiefs installed were Companion J. P. Platt, P.M.E.Z., as M.E.Z. ; Companion J. K. Digges, as H.; Companion W. R. Wass, as J. The ceremony of installa- tion being over the following officers were duly invested by Companion Platt as his officers for the ensuing 12 months, viz., Companion R. Evans, Treasurer; Companion W. Mel- lor, Scribe K; Companion William Lyon, Scribe N.; Com- panion George Pincer, Prin. S.; Companion William Houghton, Janitor. The b dance-sheet was presented and declared very satisfactory, there being a very substantial balance in hand. Brother Jas. White, J.P.M., Lodge of Equity No. 1,384, was then exalted to the supreme degree of Holy Royal Arch Masonry. Brother George Roberts, MM., of the Ellesmere Lodge, No. 758, was duly proposed as a candidate for the next chapter meeting; and the best wishes were tendered by several Companions from other chapters. From the excellent manner in which the pro- ceedings were conducted, we beve every reason to believe that this chapter will be very successful in the future, and we must congratulate the members on their selection of chiefs and officers, as they are in every way fitted for the important duties apportioned to them. ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.-.—OR Monday afternoon an accident occurred at the lower glass works of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers. As John Toole, of 26, High-street, • Eccleston, was assisting to lift a crate of glass he slipped and fell, the crate falling upon his legs, spraining one of them and inflicting other injuries of a minor character. He was conveyed in a cart to the surgery of Drq. Gaskell and Hay, and subsequently taken to the Cottage Hospital. From inquiries we have made he is now doing well. SIR R. Cnoss, M.P. ox EDUCATION.—In distributing, on Thursday, the prizes to the pupils of the Bolton Church Institute, Sir Richard Cross insisted upon the importance, not only of primary, but of secondary education. The latter, he said, was often quite as essential as elementary instruction. Sir Richard also strongly advocated a system of technical education for the working classes, this being necessary to fit them to cope with American and foreign competition. The right hon. gentleman avowed his belief in the ability of Englishmen to beat foreigners in their own fields.

I VISIT OF TIIE RIGHT 110 N. J. CHAMBERLAIN TO laympoor..—On Wednesday, the Right Hon. J. Chamber- lain,President of the Board of Trade, with a party of gentle- men, including Mr. Farrer, secretary of that department, and Sir R. Colinson, deputy master of the Trinity House,l who have been officially engaged in visiting the port of Liverpool, embarked by the Dock Board tender Vigilant, for a cruise on the river, and also to pay visits to some of the outgoing steamers for America. It is understood that the accommodation provided for steerage passengers will engage ' the special attention of these gentlemen, and the Board of Trade will also inquire into the working of the railway rates for goods to and from Liverpool, as well as into other matters of interest to the trade of the port. VOLUNTEER REVIEW AT PRESTON. —A review ef the principal volunteer corps of the county of Lancashire took place on Saturday, in the Marsh. Preston. In consequence of an inability to secure Moor Park for the purposes of the review, it became necessary to narrow the original design of the promoters of this interesting event, which had con- templated an assemblage of something like 10,000 Volunteers. The number of troops which assembled on Saturday—each corps being under full arms and accompanied by its band— amounted to about 4,000 men. In consequence of the long distances which some of the corps had to travel, the review did not commence until after four o'clock, when some 10,000 or 15,000 spectators had assembled. Owing to the unfitness of the ground for extensive evolutions, the review took the form of a brigade review, the various movements of which I were conducted without hitch until the march past, when General Cameron thought it necessary to call upon some of the men "to hold their heads up like Englishmen." In all other respects the review passed off with much credit to the officers and men.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
WEIDNESDAL—Before Messrs. J. Bibby (chairman) and Holbrook Gaskell, jun.

STREET Rows.—Rose Carney and Elizabeth McGuirk were each onieresi. to be bound over to keep the peace one month, on the evidence of P.C. Robinson for fighting in Oxford-street.—Mary Mach, for using unpolite language to a neighbour named Bridget Gill, had to enter into her own recognisances of £lO, and find one surety in £5 to keep the peace for one month. A NEGLECTED CRlLD.—Thomas Bate was summoned by the Whines School Board, who were represented by Mr. Danby, their clerk, for not having sent his child to school. —Defendant had 55., including costs, to pay. A WEAR CHARGE OF FELONY AGAINST A DOMESTIC.— Mary Keating, domestic servant, was charged, on remand, with stealing a shawl and an apron, value 2s. 6d., on the previous Friday, the property of Mrs. Noon, widow, Milton- street—Prosecutrix said the prisoner had been three wesks in her service, and on the night mentioned she went opt, leaving her in the house. On returning, at ten o'clock, she found the prisoner missing, and the shawl and apron gone. —Mr. Husband defended the prisoner, and said she alleged the prosecwrix had given her notice. Upon her leaving Mrs. Noon wanted the shawl and apron back, though she had given them to her. He submitted the case was not one of larceny, and that the woman had behaved harshly to the prisoner in taking such proceedings.—The Bench dis- missed the case.

THE THIEF AND THE COAT.—SMARTLY CAPTURED.—Jas. Dacey, described as a tramp, was charged on remand with stealing an overcoat, value 305., the property of Mr. F. 11. Pankhurst.—Richard Johnson. a gate-keeper at the Public Baths, said that on the Bth instant he was at the door of that building, and saw the prisoner coming from the direction of the prosecutor's shop, with an overcoat on his arm, similar to the one produced. Dacey put on the garment when near the London and North-Western Railway station, on which witness noticed that there was a ticket upon it. He went to Mr. Pankhurst's and found that the coat had been stolen from there.—The prosecutor was called, and said he hung the coat at his shop door at eight o'clock in the morning, and missed it about two in the afternoon. From what he heard he went to an entry and found the prisoner wearing it. He said to Dacey, " I have caught you, my man," to which he replied, "All right." The garment was worth 30s. —P.C. Strickland' proved apprehending the prisoner, who said he had been out of work and could not get any food or clothes, and was tempted t take the article.—Prisoner was committed to the Liverpold Quarter Sessions for trial. ATTEMPTING TO ROB A TILL—Joh Riley, aged 18, a tramp, was sent to gaol one month for trying to abstract, money from the till at the Ram's Head public-house. Carlile-street, on the 7th instant. Prisoner was caught in the act by Mr. Wood, and was given into the custody of P.C. Graham. FARNWORTH SHOW AND THE SPIRIT LICENSE.— MI Dove, of the Roby Hotel, who has for several years sup- plied the refreshments at the Farnworth Agricultural Show, and had accepted the contract for yesterday (Friday), ap- plied for an occasional license to sell spirits from Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, from seven in the morning to ten a night —The Chairman, after consulting with his brother magistrate, said they saw no necessity fer granting a spirit license for the day before the show, and they could not do so. They were willing to give the license for the other days, but they must restrict the hours to from ten in the morning to seven in the evening.—Mr. Dove said he had always been granted a license for the day before the show in former years, and the hours he had mentioned had been those within which he had been enabled to sell spitits. He could not accept the license on such terms.—Mr. Dove then left the court, and returned in a few minutes, stating that he should be glad if the magistrates would listen to Mr. Husbund, solicitor, in the matter.—The Chairman : If we do so we cannot alter our decision.—Mr. Dove then left the court, and up to the close of business had refused to take the license under the restriction as to hours.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday, at the Board- room, Alforde-street. Major Cross presided, and there were also present Messrs. Carey, Brown, Pankhurst, Hayes, Gasket', jun., Handley, Forster, Allen (clerk), Roberts (engineer), Higginson.(surveyor), and Dikson (imisance in- spector). THE WEST BANK PRIVATE IMPROVEMENT ACCOUNTS—IM- PORTANT COMMUNICATION. The CHAIRMAN said the members would recollect that Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., of Warrington, had been making an application to the Local Government Board, on behalf of certain clients of theirs, in regard to the West Bank sewerage private improvement accounts) with the en- deavour to cause the Board to do what they did not think was right in the matter. A letter had been received from the Local Government Board, transmitting for the information of the Board a copy of a communication which had been addressed by them to Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., solicitors, with regard to the memorial from their clients to the Board respecting the private improvement expenses. It was as follows:-.-'. Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., 9th August, 1881.—G entlemen,-1 am directed by the Local Government Boardto advert to your letter of the 13th ult, with reference to the memorial presented to them by your clients, Messrs. It. Davies and W. Hurt WI ight, respecting the action taken by the Widnes Local Board with regard to certain private improvement expenses, and to state that the Board are advised that the appeal of the memorialists cannot now be entertained under section 268 of the Public Health Act, 1875. The appeal asks, in effect, that a claim settled some time ago may he re-opened, although the payments in respect thereof have been made. The Board are advised that this cannot be done.—J. F. RorrEN, Assistant Secretary.—To Messrs. R. Davies and Co., Market-place, Warrington."
THE NEWTON, HAYDOCE AND GOLBORNE BUILDING SOCIETY
AND THE BOARD.

The following correspondence had also been received in regard to a similar matter from the Newton, Haydock and Golborne Building Society, which the Chairman read:— " Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., 9th Septem- ber, 1881,—Sir,--I ,am direct2d by the Local Government Board to transmit to you, for the consideration of the Widnes Local Board, the accompanying copy of a letter which the Board have received from the Secretary of the Newton, Haydock and Go!borne Permanent Benefit Build- ing Society, appealing against the decision of the Local Board in the matter of two demands for the payment of private expenses, and I am to request that the Board may b 3 fur- nished with the observations of the Local Board on the sub-

ject.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, J. F. Borrow, Assistant Secretary."--" Newton, Haydock and Golborne Permanent Benefit Building Society, Park-road, Newton-le- Blows, August 26th, 1881.—Sir,—I now beg to annex copies of two apportionments for private improvements made by the Widnes Local Board against this society, amounting to £B6 19s. 6d. and £6B Is. respectively, and I also annex copies of the demands for payments of same. And in be- half of the trustees and members of the above society, I hereby appeal to the Local Govern- ment Board in •London in terms of section 268 of the Public Health Act, 1875, agaidst the said apportionments and demand notes for the payment of the sums hereinbefore named, and pray your honourable Board to make such enquiry, or order, as may be considered equitable, and your petitioners will ever pray. The grounds of appeal are as follows : viz., Ist, we consider the charges excessive. 2nd, we have reason to believe they are illegally made up. 3rd, we have got no credit for the old materials. 4th, the Surveyor has refused to give us particulars as to how the sums named have been arrived at. sth, we are in- formed that interest has seen charged on the outlay prior to the demand for payment, and in certain cases that have already been decided by arbitration, the ratepayers were not allowed to put the surveyor in the witness-box, and there- fore, could not ask him the question as to interest, and as we have no confidence whatever in the Local Board of Widnes, or their surveyor, as to their mode of conducting their busi- ness, we are compelled to appeal to you, trusting you will grant this our bumble petition, I am, yOur obedient servant, JOHN ADAMS, secretary."—Major Cnoas said that the Clerk had prepared a reply, of which the following was a copy, on the subject:—" Widnes Local Board, Public Offices, Widnes, 131 h September, 1881.—Sir,—I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter, dated 9th inst., enclosin,g copy of a letter from the Secretary of the Newton, Haydock, and Golborne Permanent Building Society, appealing against the decision of this Board, in the matter of two demands for the pay- ment of private improvement expenses, and I now submit the observations of this Board, as requested. Before doing so, however, I respectfully submit that the aforesaid society are not now entitled to appeal to your Board under section 268 of the Public Health Act, 1875. The appeal should , have been made within 21 days of the ap- portionment notice, which was dated 23rd April, 1881. Should you not consider the above objection , fatal to this appeal made to you, I now proceed to I reply in detail. The Widnes Local Board having determined to pave, flag, &c., certain streets, notice was served in 1878 upon the property owners. The property owners having failed to comply with the Board's notice, it was resolved that the Board should do the work as provided for under the above-named section. Tenders were duly advertised for— the lowest was accepted—the work was completed in 1880, and the surveyor apportioned the expenses according to the frontage of the respective properties, in accordance with the I abovr-mentioned section. The apportionment upon the so- ciety in question was dated 23rd April, 1331. A notice of I dispute of apportionment, dated 11th July, 1881, written upon the paper of the aforesaid society, but not signed, has been received, which, however, this Board is willing to ac- knowledge as a valid dispute of apportionment, and I re- spectfully submit that under section 150 of the Public Health Act, 1875, the society must go to arbitration. Re- specting the various charges made by the aforesaid society, I beg to submit the following answers :-Ist and 2ucl. These would be decided by the arbitrator. 3rd. Credit notes, dated 3rd September, 1881 for £9 3s. Bd. and £5 10s. 6d., being the value of the old material, have been forwarded to the society. 4th. The surveyor has never refused to produce the apportionment slice', but he has refused to go into the question of items; and I beg respectfully to point out that he is not called upon to do so under the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875. A distinct offer in writing was made on behalf of this Board on the 9th May, 1881, to pro- duce the original apportionment sheet. This sheet sets forth the total length of the street, the' total cost, the various frontages, and the respective charge against each property. sth. Interest has been charged as part of the cost of the street, and I respectfully- submit that it should be so charged, otherwise the ratepayers at large would have to pay this expense incurred solely for the benefit of a few pro- perty owners. With respect to the cases referred to as having been lately under arbitration, and the statement that the ratepayers were not allowed to put the surveyor in the witness-box, I have to say that the surveyor gave his evi- dence before the arbitrator, and before the magistrates in open court, upon oath, and that be was in the witness-box. The solicitor who then appeared for certain ratepayers is the solicitor to the Building Society now appealing to your Board. In conclusion, I beg to say that this Board is quite prepared to refer this dispute to arbitration.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, JAMES T. ALLEN, clerk."

div.head: FLOWER QUEEN CANTATA AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE FLOWER QUEEN CANTATA AT RUNCORN.

The large and overflowing audiences which assembled on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, in the Public Hall, to listen to this charming cantata testifies to its popularity. It will be within the recollection of our readers that it was given last year by the ladies connected with Bethesda Con- gregational Chapel. On this occasion additional attraction was given to its performance by the engagement of Miss Laura Haworth, Liverpool, and Mr. B. B. Pierpoint, R.A.M., as principals, the chorus being the same with a few addi- tions. Miss Laura Haworth, "Rose," sang the music allotted to her with a grace and expression befitting the part, and was frequently applauded. She was particularly happy in the song, "Filled with gratitude and love," and was encored each evening. In several other songs also her efforts were rewarded with well merited encores. Mr. B. B. Pierpoint's "get-up" as "The Recluse" was well conceived, and was an excellent impersonation of a hermit. The sonorous tones of his fine voice told with splendid effect, and in several solos he was raptu- rously encored. Amongst the solists, Miss E. Ainsworth as " Crocus " was loudly applauded, and it was evident the audience intended it to be taken as an en- core, but the next solo," Dahlia," follows so closely as to preclude it being responded to. The duet, "Rose and lily,' sung by Miss L. Haworth and Miss Handley, was very effec- tive. Miss Littler's solo," Sunflower," was sung with great animation, and was a most telling number, the accompany- ing chorus being well rendered. Miss Wright and Miss Rhodes, in the characters of "Hollyhock " and "Dande- lion," were greeted with much applause. We may say that all the solos were highly appreciated by the audience. The greater part of the choruses were rendered in an efficient manner, especially the concluding one " Light of eternal love." The sleeping scene, " When the poppies lull the flowers to sleep," appeared to be much appreciated, the coloured lights thrown on having a very pleasing effect. Mr. Earp displayed considerable skill in the flute obbligate in imitation of the nightingale. Miss Jukes as pianist, and Mr. J. W. Joule, as harmoniumist, contributed largely to the success of the performances by the excellent manner in which all the accompaniments were executed. The floral decorations were carried out under the direction of Mr. G. Rhodes, who was assisted by Mr. T. E. Tunna, Miss Littler, Miss F. Littler, Miss Williams, Miss Edwards, Miss Morris, Misses Catherall, Mrs. Thomas, Mrs. W. Handley, and a number of other willing workers connected with the congre- gation. The platform, which was enlarged for the occasion, presented a very charming appearance by large numbers of beautiful plants, ferns, and flowers kindly lent by gentle- men in the neighbourhood. We understand that the ferns and evergreens were obtained, by permission, from Helsby Hill and Flood Brooks; these gave the platform the appear- ance of a dell in the forest where fairies love to dwell. Mr. urdly W. Handley conducted the musical portion with marked ability, and the numerous movements of the singers in their exits and entrances were under the control of Mr. T. E Tunna. We are informed that the proceeds after deducting eN' eni ng by d M l-deserved encore being awarded to Mrs. expenses, will be devoted to the Minister's House Fund, ,wvenriech we trust will be a substantial sum. div.head: WIDNES METHODISM,
div.p: WIDNES METHODISM,

PUBLIC TEA MEETING AT OAKLAND-STREET. On Wednesday afternoon a public tea meeting was held ' in the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Oakland-street, Widnes, in aid of the Trust Fund, aad also to welcome the Rev. J. H. Cummings, the newly appointed superintendent I minister. A capital tea was provided, to which about 200 persons sat down. The tables were presided over by the following ladies, whom' it may be observed, are all members I of the Sunday school in connection with Oakland-street Chapel :—Mrs. Frodsham, Mrs. Wendt, Mrs. Croft, Mrs. Harper, Mrs. Jackson, and the Misses Jones, Whitby, Anker, Rogers, Brooks, Hartland, and Youd. After tea a public I meeting was held, Mr. Robert Shaw, of Runcorn, presiding. There were also present on the platform the Revs. J. H. Cumming and J. Tessyman, and Messrs. Thos. Sadler, Thos. Whitby, and Wm. Hartland.—The Cuaramati said he was very pleased to see so large an attendance, because it showed I Mr. Cummings that they sympathised with him and welcomed him to his new sphere of labour. They must I remember that Widnes had nothing attractive about itself, ald that it would no doubt be a trial to Mr. Cummings to come to a place of which he had no doubt heard before in not a very favourable sense. The only things that could be I at all attractive in Widnes were the smiling faces which I greeted Mr. Cummings on every hand. He advised them not to stay at home and wonder when the new minister was going to pay them a visit, for even ministers felt a certain degree of diffilence in visiting the houses of strangers, although they were members of their congre- gations. The proper thing for them to do, according to etiquette, was to take the first opportunity of paying their new pastor a visit, and thus indicate to him that lie was j thoroughly welcome in their midst.—Mr. HARTLAND, on 1 rising, said he was very pleased that they had got so good a substitute in the place of their late minister, Mr. Bingant. They had heard Mr. Cummings once, but that night they had met to give him a special welcome. He thought it was , the duty of everyone to rally round the minister and to do , their utmost to cause the church to prosper. It was not the proper thing to leave all the work to the minister. A great deal might be, and actually was being done by the force of ' example. For instance, a member of a " class " invariably looked round for his class leader at the week-night services, and if lie did not see him he came to the conclusion that it was not necessary for him to attend either. In giving his financial report, Mr. Hartland said that before Sunday last they had a balance of about £2, and he thought that the services on that day and the proceedings from the meeting that night would swell this already large sum to about £7. They received from the pew rents something like £lO per annum, and 10 also from the Sunday school, making a total of £27. On the other hand, there was £6 to be paid as interest for borrowed money. The collectors had obtained between £4O and £5O for the purpose of paying off the debts, but £l2O was required. Nine shillings and sevenpence was paid yearly for ground rent, and about £l5 for lighting, dm., of the chapels, so that the report was not at all cheering, and an earnest effort ought to be made to clear the chapel of the debts. He still hoped that something might be done, and that the present genera- tion would see a new edifice in the place of the present one, which was rather incommodious—Mr. T. Sd-DLER, referring to the growth of Methodism in Widnes, said that it had made considerable progress during his remembrance. At one time, the only place of worship they were possessed of was a small room over two cottages: but now they had the Victoria-road chapel and the place which they now occu- pied, besides out side spots. He thought the progress already made ought to stimulate them to go on, for what , they had accomplished was only an earnest of what they might do with renewed efforts.—The Rev. J. TERRYMAN said he did not think speech-making was his forte. What his utterance that night would be, whether a sermon, a lecture, or a discourse, he would leave them to determine. That meeting was the chapel anniversary, but after the facts ' had been uttered that the chapel was scarcely half large enough, that they had a very excellent school which would fill the building, and that the chapel was crowded on a Sunday, what more remained to be said? He had heard the saying, that there was nothing new under the sun, but he thought that a minister without faults would be a new thing. He knew that he was not without them, and he asked them to sympathise with and pray for him and his. new superintendent. There was a great deal th be done before Widnes was evangelised. The teeming multitudes of men and women who never entered a place of worship; the use of profane language, which seemed to him to be worse in Widnes than in any other town, all went to show that the place was in a very bad condition, and that something must be done for it. A time.would come when Christ would tell them what he had suffered for them, and say, "What bast thou done for me ?" He (the speaker) left them to answer the question themselves.—The Rev. J. H. Cumsrpscts thanked the meet- ing and the previous speakers for the very hearty and kind reception they had given him. He felt that both the minis- ters and the congregation had a sacred trust committed to I them in the system of the church government which they believed to be the right one, and it was their duty to build it up and make it more powerful and efficient as an agent to accomplish the salvation of the people. He would like all present to catch the spirit of old Methodism which ani- mated Wesley. It was no new doctrine that they were to believe; it was the same " old, old, story of Jesus and His love," which they were to carry abroad. There was a great power in prayer, and it was the duty as well as the privi- lege of everyone to pray as well as work. He felt sure that if they acted upon this plan they could not fail to succeed, not only in getting larger congregations, but ultimately a more commodious chapel, for it was a well-known Raying that " God helped those who helped themselves."—Mr. T. WHITLEY said something had been remarked about money matters. He was quite at a loss to know how the deficiencies were to be made good, as many of the present seat-holders were leaving the chapel on account of its inconvenience. He often felt he should like to invite persons to visit them, but that meant turning some one else out, as they could easily fill the place without the regular attendants. He very much regretted having to make such a statement, but it was nevertheless true ; and it was essential that something be done in the matter.—The CHAIRMAN advised the committee to take a room in the Board schools, and institute a children's service. He said that was the method adopted id a:most all the large towns, and as the cost would not be very great he thought the plan might be carried out with advantage, as it would then leave the chapel free for adult worshippers.—During the evening the choir, accompanied on the harmonium by Mr. William Whitby, sang several anthems. Great praise is due to Mr. Whitby for the way in which he led the singing, which was really well worth hearing.—After the usual votes of thanks I had been passed, the choir sang " ()nen ye the gates," and ' the proceedings then terminated.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.'
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.'

These minutes which were approved, on the motion of Mr. GASLELL, seconded by Mr. BROWN (with the exception of one item about the proposed sale of a horse), showed that there was a decrease of 4,544,170 gallons in the quantity of water delivered during the four weeks ending August 24th, as compared with the corresponding period last year, and a decrease of 303,000 cubic feet in the gas sent out during the same time. The Ann-street east drainage question had been considered. The engineer informed the committee that the gas yard drainage was now pumped away, owing to existing levels, and that consequently, he had taken means to prevent the surface drainage from flowing into the street. The committee could not see their way to altering existing ar- rangements.

div.head: HIGHWAY MATTERS.
div.p: HIGHWAY MATTERS.

The minutes of the Highway Committee were adopted on the proposition of Mr. Kershaw, seconded by Mr. Handley. It appeared from them that Mr. Brock, on behalf of the School Board, having explained to the Chairman of the committee that certain land was given up on condition that the whole of the flagging should be done at the schools, it had been resolved that the entrance to the doorways in Milton-street should be flagged. Mossbank-road was now reported as completed by the railway company; and it had been decided that upon the railway company paying the ex- pense incurred the road should be adopted. Nothing had been done, as yet, by the railway companies to make their bridges water-tight overhead.—The following agreements were ordered to be signed :—With Mr.Allcard, for widening Marsh Hall-lane; the Runcorn Property and Investment Company and Mr. Allcard for widening Lower House-lane; Milton Chapel Trustees for widening Widnes and Milton- roads.
HEALTH OF THE TOWN. -THE FAIR QUESTION AGAIN,-A

CASTING VOTE. The Health Committee reported that there had been seven deaths from typhoid fever during the month in John. street, Simm's Cross, Albert-road, Oxlord and Major Cross streets. The Medical Officer's report showed that the birihs had been 75, or 36 per 1,000; the deaths 40, or 19.2 per 1,009, including 15 of children under one year, four of children between one and five years, and 15 from zymotic diseases.—The Nuisance Inspector reported four cases of typhoid fever under treatment on the 6th inst. The Inspector had been instructed to enquire about the vessel upon which J. Varndell worked at the time he was attacked by smallpox, and to take steps to prevent her corn- ing to Widnes again until disinfected. The Surveyor and Inspector were to report as to wooden or other erections in back yards, and the extent of clear space in such yards. It was recommended that provisions be made in the new bye- laws for the appointment of a town crier for the township at a fixed rate of charge, and that no other person be allowed to exercise the vocation. The market receipts for August were £l2 14s. Bd., being a decrease of £3 10s. 2d. upon the amount received in the correspond'ng period of last year. —Mr. CAREY, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he believed he was correct in saying that they might con- sider themselves tolerably secure from any smallpox cases arising in the Widnes centre for some time to come. He paidsa high compliment to the'severe precautions .taken.by the family affected to Iffevtnt the-disesserpeadin,g.—Mf. , MATTHEWS proposed, and Mr. PANKIICRST seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. BnowN said he saw that the time for holding the fair had been fixed for the end of the month. He felt bound to say that he was of opinion it was most undesirable that such a gathering should be held in the town, especially in these dull times. He moved that

the fair should not be advertised, as the minutes proposed, and that the Board's servants take no steps with the object of bringing the people associated with it to Widnes....... Mr. HANDLEY said the office of tovan crier was a very ancient one, and he believed that it had been in the Shep- herd family, to which the resolution of the committee re- ferred, for three generations.—Mr. PA/MI=ST remarked that as the question of holding the fair had again come up, he must withdraw his name from the resolution approving of the minutes. He should second the amendment moved by Mr. Brown —Mr. CAREY scarcely knew what course the committee could pursue on this question in order that the Board might be satisfied. On the the last occasion when it came up, the committee distinctly agreed not to advertise the fair, an deference to the feeling of the gentlemen who were members of the committee, and that portion of the public who objected to it being held. When, however, the conarnittee placed the motion before the Board, in the minutes, for approval, they upset it and decided that the fair should be advertised! Under these circumstances, the committee had, he presumed, determined to advertise, and it would remain with the Board to say whether they approved of this course or not. Personally; he did not care which course was decided upon, as he did not apprehend it would make any difference. He must ask Dr. O'Keeffe to give an explanation as to the town crier. He (the Speaker) really did not thiuk they needed any such public official.—Mr. MarrnEws did not know any valid reason why the businessl of crier should be left open to any one who choose to enter it.—Dr. &KEEFER did not see whv the Board should adopt a different plan this year in dealing with the fair, to that which they had pursued in former years. No doubt the times were bad—unfortunately they were all prepared to make this admission—but if the members decided to support the amendment moved by Mr. Brown, they would stultify themselves. If they had a fair in the town at all, why should not they endeavour to make it a success? Really it was not for the benefit of their noble selves that they were getting up this fair, but in order to do some little to diminish the total amount of the rates. He was afraid that those gentlemen who opposed the holding of it were ac- tuated more by a desire for public notoriety than their duty to the ratepayers. He did not like any gentleman upon that Board showing a lack of perfect independence in his course of action, confident that he could vindicate his proceedings to the ratepayers, if called upon to do so. It was all very well for those who were opposed- to the fair to say it was thoroughly demoralising, but he did not believe in the truth- fulness of such a statement. If fairs were demoralising, what caused the authorities in St. Helens, Warrington, or Proud Preston to allow them to be carried on. In fact, in nearly every part of England fairs were held, and he was of opinion that there was certainly an absence of immorality at the Widnes one, thanks to the surveillance of the constabu- lary. He should certainly either support the proposition to advertise the fair, or do away with it altogether—he cared not which. He should be satisfied whichever course was adopted. As to the town crier, he believed it was the cus- to n of all corporations to have such an official, and be had heard opinions from many ratepayers in favour of the desirabiliry of the town having one. In fact, he believed it was owing to the expression of this opinion that the matter was brought before the last meeting of the Health Com- mittee. Before sitting down he might say in reference to boxing, that though the science was considered a noble one, it had been thought better not to have the professors of it upon the ground.—Mr. CAREY proposed another amend- ment, which was duly seconded, to the effect that the propo- sals as to the sewer in Lower House-lane should not be car- ried out for another month.—Mr. BnowN said that last year the committee decided they would not advertise the fair, but at the promptings of one of the members of the Board who was so terribly independent and fearless as to any remarks that might be made outside, it was decided to advertise. Dr. O'Keeffe had referred to the case of St. Helens, but he (Mr. Brown) was prepared to maintain that the Town Council of that town were desirous of doing away with the fair, and had requested the person who held the land not to permit it to be held there again. As to the profit made from the holding of it, it was out of all propor- tion to the sum it took out of the pockets of the shop- keepers. In fact, the fair did not either add to the material or moral prosperity of Widnes in the slightest degree.—The CHAIRMAN called Mr. Brown's attention to the fact that the greatest objection to the holding of the fair in St. Helens was that it took place upon private grounds, Iso that the Corporation were prevented from having that supervision over it which they would like.— Mr. Bnowx: I believe they do not favour it as a Corpora- tion.—Dr. ()TEEPEE said it would be a new departure on the part of the Board if they did not advertise.—Mr. HAYES : It will be the first time that it has not been advertised.—Mr. BROWN: No, it wont. The Board has followed the same course I am recommending before.—Mr: DICKSON (inspector) in reply to a question, said the fair had always been advertised in the paet.—Mr. KERSHAW moved, and Mr. MarrirEws seconded, an amendment in favour of the recommendation as to the appointment of a town crier being struck out of the minutes. This amendment was car- ried unanimously, with the exception of Mr. Handley.— The amendment in favour of the minutes passing, with the exception of the part relating to Lower House-lane was then put, and carried without dissent.—The Canntax then put the amendment of Mr. Pankhurst on the fair question, on which five members voted for and five against it.—The Csammart: I give my casting vote in favour of the fair being advertised as usual. (Laughter.)
FINANCE.

These minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. HAYES, seconded by Mr. GASKELL, and showed that instructions had been given to press for payment of all private improve- ment accounts within seven days, or have legal proceedings taken for their recovery. The apportionment sheets for the paving, drc., of the following streets had been submitted : Bank-street, £623 10s. 4d.; Cholmondley-street, .£1,989 Os. 66.; Oakland-street, £736 12s. 66.; Terrace-road, £682 Os. ld. It was resolved that the various property owners be debited with these sums. Loans amounting to £6,300 had been received on water extension account since the last I report. I

MR. STANDLEY ON THE LW/EL OROSSINO NUISANCL Mr. HANDLEY said that two months ago the questios of level crossings was brought somewhat prominently before the notice of the Board. This was more particularly the case with regard to Waterloo-road crossing ; and he might say that the nuisance at this place appeared to become worse week by week. When the matter was last brought forward the Chairman said it was being enquired into, and he should like to know whether anything definite had been done.— The CHAIRMAN thought the question a very proper one, for he did Hot see that the London and North-Western Railway Company were taking any steps whatever to erect bridges over the three level crossings where they had agreed to place them. If Mr. Handley had no objection he would move that the clerk be instructed to write to the railway company asking them when they intended to proceed with the erection of the bridges at Farnworth, Appleton, and Lugsdale level crossings. He believed it was now nearly twelve months since the railway company signed the agree- ment to proceed with this work. He was receiving constant complaints from ratepayers about the way in which the Waterloo and Anne-street crossings were opened and closed. He absolved Mr. Shaw, the general traffic manager of the company, from any blame, because he believed that gentle- man had dose everything in his power to see that the gates were kept open as long a time as possible, but it was only natural that the railway men should give the preference to their own engines. As a matter of fact, the public in Widnes were being constantly prejudiced in their work owing to the existence of the level crossings. He was de- cidedly of opinion that the rail way company should be asked to do away with them altogether. It might be said that the Anne-street crossing was not of very much importance. but he did not see that the Board had any right to ignore even the comparatively fewer number of people who used that crossing, and who were, undoubtedly, putto much incon- venience.—lt was decided, unanimously, and without the ne- cessity of any formal r2solution, that the Clerk should write to the London and North-Western Railway Company asking when they intended to proceed with the erection of the bridges; calling their attention to the 'Waterloo and Anne- street crossings particularly, and expressing the emphatic opinion of the Board that the nuisance complained of could only be remedied by the erection of bridges.

div.head: FINANCING EXTRAORDINARY.
div.p: FINANCING EXTRAORDINARY.

The CHAIRMAN said it would be in the recollection of the Board that a sum of £B,OOO had been overcharged for the maintenance of the highways, and it was decided that the Surveyor should look into the matter. Mr. Higginson had brought forward a statement by which he corrected the ex- penditure on roads and for public improvements by £2,459 us. 3d. This was certainly something towards the £BOOO, but it still left about £5,500 as being said to have been spent in the maintenance of the roads during the last three years. This money had, however been spent on general ac- Count; it had certainly never been expended on the im- provement of the roads ; and if it had been used in another manner, it ought to have been included in a special account. The anditor would be in Widnes again within a 'few days. and perhaps the members of the Finance Committee Would undertake a further investigation on the subject —Mr. HAYES : If we cannot prove that it has been spent, we shall have to lay a rate for it.—The CHAIRMAN: The investiga• tion made by Mr. Higginson proves that, to a certain ex- tent, our conjectures are right. What will you do about it, Mr. Kershaw P—Mr. KERSHAw : It is beyond our scope, unless we agree to come here and spend weeks in examining the books.—Tbe CHAIRMAN: No person can know am-- thing about it but the Surveyor. He proposes only to charge this item of £2,459 and let the other go. What does he propose to do with the other?— Mr. HIGOINSON : It would have to come out of the rates.— Mr. KERSHAW : I cannot see that we can do anything with the matter but send it back to the surveyor and accountant. —The CHAIRMAN: It is no good sending it back, as the auditor is coming on the sth. It is certainly the Highway Committee's business.—Mr. KERSHAW: Perhaps you will pass this, and then we will try to deal with the other.—The CHAIRMAN: I take it, then, that the Board agree that the £2,459 Hs. 3d. of the amounts which have been charged igainst general account shall be charged to public improve- ments, it having been proved to their satisfaction that it has been so spent —lt may be well to add that the question in- volved in the above discussion is not so serious as might at first sight appear. There is no dispute as to the money having been spent, but it has been charged to the wrong account, and has thus produced the muddle referred to.

HARVEST PROSPECTS IN WALES.—The fine weather of the past few days has done much towards the gathering in of the gehmtops in Anglesey and Carnarvonshire, and it is expected that the harvest will be a good one, the straw being long with full ear. ,Potatoes seem to be the only vegetable that has suffered much from the incessant rain some short time back.

- - - - The Methodist (Ecumenical Conference was resumed in London for the eighth time on Thursday. The Rev. Douglas, of the Methodist Church of Canada, presided, and the question discussed was the use of the press for the ad. vancement of Christianity.

The movement designed to check those who are respoli. Bible for the " corner " in the Liverpool cotton market cOll.. tinues to spread. A number of mills at Blackburn, Damen, Church, and the neighbourhood were stopped on Thursday. At a meeting of representatives of limited companies held at Oldham on Thursday evening a resolution was unani- mously passed agreeing to stop the mills for a week.

_ SELL/Na A PIIBLIC HOSPITAL.—In consequence of legal proceedings taken to restrain the Heywood Town Council from further using their fever hospital for patients, the building has been abandoned, and on Thursday night it was offered by sale by auction. The hospital buddings cost the town over £1,100; the highest bid nas .£195, at which price the property was withdrawn.

The Central News has received the following telegram from the Right Hon. James Lowther ye:terday :—A speech alleged in some of to-day's newspapers to have been de- livered by me in Westmoreland is erroneously attributed to me. I have spoken nowhere for ten days. At Marylebone revision, yesterday, Mr. Wood asked whether the case of Mr. Gladstone's vote was now disposed ' of with the exception that the revising barrister would con- sider what hour he should grant a case for the superior court. The revising barrister intimated that be should re- serve the whole question. Mr. Wood said if be decided not to strike the name off the list he should ask for a case on behalf of the Conservatives.

The adjourned inquest on the bodies of the persons who lost their lives in the disastrous railway collision at Black.. burn on the Bth of August, was concluded yesterday. Additional evidence was taken, and the jury found a verdict of accidental death. The cause of the collision they agreed was the loose working of the signals, and the excessive speed at which the Manchester express was being driven into the station. The jury were also of opinion there , should be more precaution to the trains than the east and west cabins afforded. No blame attached to anyone.

The fire was still raging in Pentre Colliery on Thursday, but fortunately—contrary to the first reports—all the men had been rescued. A Cardiff telegram says all the men were rescued through the downcast shaft. A party of explorers descended the pit directly after the fire broke out, the first men to be reached being those working in the two hundred feet seam. The explorers afterwards penetrated the six feet seam, where many of the men were found in an unconscious and half suffocated condition: but, owing to the prompt manner in which help was forthcoming, not a single life was sacrificed. The survivors state that the timbers near the boilers, some eight yards from the bottom of the shaft, caught fire, and a dense volume of smoke penetrated the six feet seam. There is now some danger of the roof falling.

The Land League Convention was opened in Dublin, on Thursday, Mr.' Parnell in the chair. Upwards of a thousand delegates were present. Telegrams from various parts of the United States were as follow: "Hold the harvest." "No rent." "If you submit to the Gladstone sham, sub- scriptions will cease." "One step backwards, and no more money." "In the name of God, humanity, and truth, no rents, no surrender." "Down with landlordism, and down for ever." "The cause of Ireland is the cause of America." 6' If you pay a rent, no help from this country." "Strict adherence to the principles of the Land League, or no more help from here." Mr. Parnell, in his opening address, said that foremost among the resolutions to be submitted to them was one dealing with the question of self-govern- ment. They never could settle that question until the question of how much rent the tenant had to pay the landlord was finally settled. Whatever the tenants did under the Land Act, let them do it as one man. Let them avoid all isolated action, and let no tenant be satis- fied until all were satisfied. As regarded the labourers, if there was any failure of employment in the coming minter through the fault of the farmers, he pledged hi ~self to take his stand at the head of a labourers' movement. If they organised themselves to protect their manufactures, depend upon it they would flourish in Ireland. The great thing, in his opinion, was to resolve that they would use no articles of English manufacture whatever. There were many things they could not buy in Ireland, but let them buy them any- where but in England. Mr. Sexton, M.P., proposed, and Mr. O'Kelly, M.P., seconded a series of thirteen resolutions dealing with Home Rale, the Coercion Act, the abolition of landlordism, unity of action, provision for labourers, Irish manufacture, and other subjects. The convention adjourned till to-day, MORE SCENES AT THE TRADES UNIOIS ICONGRESS, THE POLICE FORBIDDEN TO INTERFERE.

I The annual Trades Union Congress resumed its sitting at St. Andrew's Hall, London, yesterday. Some discussion arose on the confirmation of the previous day's minutes with reference to the expulsion of the Birmingham delegates, Mr. Williams (Birmingham) wishing it to be recorded that he had moved that Messrs. Maddocks and Harlow should be allowed to remain and attend the Congress. The Chairman intimated that he could not accept the suggestion, and the matter dropped. Mr. Shorrocks moved, and Mr Ashton seconded, a resolution as to the desirability of increasing the number of factory and workshop inspectors. It was stated, that factories and workshops were often ia a most unsatisfactory and unsanitary condition, that ne number of inspectors was insufficient and inadequate for the amoufit Of Wink to be done, and that wernen should be eligible to act as inspeetors as well as men. The resolution was agreed to. The auditor's account, which showed an in- come of £837, an expenditures of £623, and a balance in hand of £213, was accepted and agreed to. At this stage Mr. King announced that two of the delegates who had been expelled, Messrs. Peters and Lind, had just forced their way past the door-keeper and re-entered the room (cries of "Turn them out"). Mr. Wilson, amidst great uproar and confusion, moved that the two men named be immediately expelled (cheers). This was seconded by several people in different parts of the room. The Chairman, amidst great excitement, put the motion to the meeting, which he declared carried unanimously. As Messrs. Peters and Lind showed no signs of going, but retained their places, Mr. Lind sitting at one of the tables, and Mr. Peters standing at the back of the room, the chairman called for volunteers to assist the door-keeper in removing them from the room (great excitement). Mr. Davidson: Do not resort to forcible expulsion; if they do not retire let it go back to their constituents. Mr. Peters: You say we have got none.—Mr. Fanbaime attempted to address the meeting but could not be heard.- -The Chairman: I again request Mr. Peters and Mr. Lind to leave the room. (Cries of "Turn them out.")—Mr. Peters: I shall not leave until I am forcibly ejected. lam one of the delegates sent here, and I have a right to remain.—Mr. Evans (London) : I move that a policeman be sent for to remove them. (Cries of " chair " and "Yes, send for the police.")—Mr. Marmott (Sheffield) : I take it this is a part of a preconcerted plan to disturb this meeting. Unless you ' are prepared to exercise your authority and eject these men from the Congress I am afraid that what they have don* in the past will be repeated to-day. The whole Congress has been upset by them. We should at once put our foot down firmly. If they have no right here they should be ejected.—The Chairman: If you will sit down quietly I will tell you what I have done. I have simply sent for the police—cheers)— and on their arrival they will be ejected. (Renewed cheers.)— Mr. Carling (Durham Miners): Not one word more of our business until these men are ejected ought ro be uttered.. I think that we should show a bold front and defy any in- truders from obstructing us in our business. It appears to me they have come to try and bring disgrace upon the Trades Unions of this country, and it is our duty not to allow them to do it.—Mr. Shorrocks (Manchester) at this moment entered the hall, and stated that Captain Bedford Pim, who was outsidej, declared that he, as a magistrate, would not allow the police to be sent for. Mr. Shorrocks asked the chairman to give him leave to remove Captain Pim.—The Chairman stated that the meeting would be ad- journed until two o'clock.—The discussion, however, ex- citedly continued amid occasional shouts of "Turn them out I "—Mr. Henry Crompton suggested they should send a deputation to the Home Office and ask for advice as to secur- ing order, in the hopes that definite instructions might be givento the police.—Some further discussion foil owed, and then a deputation was appointed to proceed to the Home Office, and the Congress adjourned until two o'clock.

At Two o'clock the Congress resumed, and the offending delegates were once more requested to withdraw. Mr. Lind, the only one present, however, protested, and amidst a scene of great uproar and excitement he was forcibly ex- pelled from the room.—Mr. Broadhurst then informed the meeting that instead of going to the Home Secretary, the deputation had asked the advice of the Magistrate at Marlborough-street Police Court, who had told them they had a perfect right to eject the objectionable delegates. A resolution was then passed censuring Captain Bedford Pun for his conduct in aiding and abetting certain persons to create a disturbance in the congress, such conduct being incompatible with his duty as a justice of the peace. The resolution was ordered to be reported to the Lord Chancel- lor. After the expulsion of Mr. Lind, business was got through quietly until the standing orders committee reported other delegates present who were not eligible, Mr. Hopkin, of the Bristol Trades Council, who was not paid by his trade and Mr. Parish, of the London Brush Makers, who had admitted he paid his own expenses. These two, upon a motion being duly carried, were ordered to withdraw, but Mr. Griffin. of Glasgow, whose case was not considered proved, remained. The Congress then adjourned.

div.p: beneficent demonstrations and institutions that are honoured I by the sanction and the presence of royalty owe none of their succesq to that presence; and of course the only ob- ject in all this is the " delectation of the upper ten," isn't it, oh! ill-used democrats ? If Mr. Peers would study the papers a little more carefully he would not doubt my state- ment that royalty "works hard for the good of the coun- try." He would see that it is constantly occupied in some good word or deed and I think he would come to pretty much the same conclusion as the Radical paper did (for even Radical papers tell the truth occasionally) when it made the heir apparent exclaim:— ~ For though as Prince of Wales, , I draw a thumping screw, Yet for it I must work As hard, my friends, as you!"

I think the case he cites to throw ridicule on my statement that our soldiers can fight and die better for a common sovereign than they could for a republican section was singular unfortunate. The idea I intended to convey, was, that if our Government were republican and the party in power. declared war, the soldiers of the opposite party, dis- agree.ing with the objects of the war, might scruple to take • part 19 it, and thus no reliance could be placed upon our army in time of need; but under a limited mon achy soldiers of both parties could without the slightest sacrifice of con- viction, fight gallantly, not for the opinions and the policies of their political opponents, but for the honour of their com- mon sovereign. Thus unity of purpose and enthusiasm in a cause dear alike to all would ensure discipline, courage and capability in our defenders. As to the great war in the United States, I should never think of insinuating that either Northeners or Southerners did not fight bravely for their re- spective causes; but if there had been the golden link of monarchy to bind them together might it not have happened that their antagonism would have been softened—they would have felt that they were all subjects of the same monarch and have refused to engage in fratricidal warfare, and thus their differences might have been settled without resorting to the terrible arbitrament of the sword ? How- ever, as I have:said, these are but incidental reasons in favour of our monarchical system—the greater arguments in its favour your correspondent has had the prudence to avoid questioning. We have already seen that the duties of royalty are not, as he seems to imagine, confined to giving assent to parliamentary bills. And as to the Queen's exercise of the power of veto, the knowledge that she has that power and that the second estate of the realm has the same power in itself imposes a check upon revolutionary measure and so leavens them as to render its exercise unnecessary. Thus under the "checks and counterchecks of our system," the violence of the revolutionary is tempered by the more Con- servative and cautious elements ofsthe constitution; and as the vessel, with the wind filling her sails on one side avid the waters resisting on the other, slips between the contending forces with grace and safety, so the ship of state wi!li the howling wind of democracy on one side, and the solid waters of monarchy and aristocracy on the other, glides smoothly and prosperously between the two, "quiet from the fear of evil."—l am, &c, ARTHUR BENNETT. iber, 1851.

Sir,—May I be allowed-t-o7nake an appeal to the Sanitary Committee? About this time last year we had the scarlet fever in Manchester-lane. Children from two families were taken to the hospital; death ensued in one case. This year we have had quite a number of cases, and every one is asking the reason for so much sickness in what should be the healthiest part of the town. May I venture upon an answer to this? And herein lies my appeal to the Sanitary Committee—the drains want cleaning. From the grids near Mr. Foster's cottage the stench is enough to poison the —. —Yours, &c., HENRY WHITHAM. Warrington.
