THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 17, 1881.
Xettet,s to the {sditor.
WORKHOUSE ECONOMY AS PRACTISED AT PRESCOT UNION.

Sir,—For some months past two paupers have been en- gaged erecting a stone fence or boundary wall, separating the workhouse premises from the high road leading to Whiston, but the work ceased about a month ago, and on making enquiry as to the Cd 119.3 of this I learn it is owing to the Revision Committee sending adrift the men engaged on the work. If this be true I cannot commend the Guar- dians forming that committee, either for the wisdom dis- played or their notions of economy, for if the Board intend finishing the wall and have to employ paid hands they will have to pay 4s. or 45. 6d. per day at least. Perhaps some Guardian will enquire into the matter for the satisfaction of Yours, tc., GASTRONOMY. • Eccleston, 7th Sept., ISSL

- • . RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEB A.TING SOCIETY. Sir,—On coming to reside at Runcotu. at the beginning of the year, I was glad to learn (but only too late to then become a member) that an institution of the above kind ex- isted here, having previous to that time taken an active part In two of the largest societies of the kind in the country. Nothing in my opinion beats them for politically educa- ting, training, and making good speakers of the younger portion of the community, who at no distant date, will no doubt have to govern the communities to which they belong. As a means also of self-cultivation, and the gaining of ac- curate knowledge of facts, they are to all taking part therein, highly advantageous, and I shall see with pleasure early public announcement of the opening of an "Autumn and win- ter session." Last year, I understand, the meetings were fortnightly, but I fail to see, why like Liverpool and others, they should not be weekly. I also noticed in a letter in a ontemporarY last week, that a committee stage has also c been the rule, but I quite agree with the writer that such is superfluous, and apt to take away th, interest that springs from the introduction of good motions, bills, (Szc. The next session at all events, need not suffer from scope, there being no dearth of subjects; the policy of the Government, Ireland, Free Trade, Protec- tion, &c., waiting I hope to be ably and exhaustively dis. cussed, and probably (who knows?) Runcorn will legislate in prospective, for the Imperial body when they meet. Hoping for in all ways a prosperous session, I remain yours truly, AN INTENDING NEW MEMBER.
FAIR TRADE ALIAS PROTECTION, VERSUS FREE

TRADE. Sir,—There can be no doubt in the minds of those who are taking notice of passing events that the defenders of Free Trade must be up and doing. We find the supporters of this policy invariably in that class of politicians termed Liberals; occasionally, he is a Tory, but then he would sink his politics at his party's bidding. I propose to take a slight view of some of the reasons now being urged against Free Trade. Before doing so, allow me to remark that I find great fault with "Fair Traders" for using such a term. Surely Mr. Cobden was a fair trader. John Bright would hardly call himself an unfair trader. Let us haVe the argu- ment fairly placed before us. Is it to be protection, recipro- city, or retaliation? James Lowther, just elected by the farmers of North Lincolnshire, states that he is "thoroughly opposed to Free Trade, he never believed in it, and that it was a mistake from the first." This means protection, and so far is honest. Placed beside this statement we have a letter in the Standard from a "North Lincolnshire farmer and voter," urging that 2s. per quarter should be placed on foreign corn. At a Fair Trade meeting held in London recently one speaker was in favour of Is., so that we see plainly the position is this, viz.: Our Conservative Maids mean Fair Trade until the Literals are turned out of office, when they would at once drop it; or else, if honest, they mean protection, and consequently taxing the people's bread. Now I prefer taking the latter proposition. The question is sufficiently important for us to be honest all round. The simple and silly fashion in which Mr. Webster handled the question at the Public Hall revealed only one thing, that was, he was there to do a bit of special pleading for Sir Gilbert, as that gentleman was unable to do it for himself. Had Mr. Webster, or "One who leYeS hi l Coen- try more than a theory," read the his- tory—l mean the domestic, not the military history —of England, for the forty years previous to the repeal of the Corn Laws, they would be aware of this his- torical fact, that, although we had navigation laws, and almost every trade in the country protected, the British workman was hell starved, thoroughly pauperised, and was constantly rioting under the command of "Captain Swing." In Carlisle a fourth of the population was bordering on starvation, nay, must actually die of famine unless relieved by extraordinary exertions. In the woollen districts of Wiltshire the allowance to the independent labourer was not two-thirds of the minimum in the workhouse. In Stock- port more than half of the master spinners had failed before the close of 1842 ; dwelling-houses to the number of 3,000 were shut up; tradesmen said "New clothes had become Out of the question among their customers, and they bought only remnants and patches to mend the old ones." Pro- tection meant in those days, and would mean again, not only misery to the nation, but the seas would be covered with smugglers and revenue cutters; we should the "good old days" back again, with a vengeance. We are told that the trade of the country is passing into other hands, and that the people are worse off than they used to be when we had pro- tection. If these two statements are true the free trader must give in. If not, the protectionist will have failed to prove his theory. It is not desirable to take any single year since 1846—the whole period is only slightly over a generation. During the 35 years the prosperity of the nation was never greater. We got rid of the navigation laws. The consequence was, nearly the whole of the carrying trade of the world came into our hands, and there remains. Mr. Gladstone's financial scheme, in 1853, included, amongst other reforms, the total remission of imposts on 133 articles. In 18E0, butter, cheese, &c., were admitted free ; in 1869 the , small duty left on corn was abolished; in 1874, sugar was relieved. Among the articles which we receive from abroad there is hardly one that reciprocity can lay bold of. Ninety- one per cent, of what we import consists of raw materials, to tax which is out of the question; and the 9 per cent, of manufactured goods—which is all that the world supplies to us—afford too feeble a leverve to work with. I hope you will allow me to give a few more reasons next week why both capitalist and workman should steadily resist protec- tionism, which calls itself by the specious name of " Fair Trade." CLIFFORD DIX.

MONARCHY IN RELATION TO THE EMPIRE. Sir,—lf I were so disposed I might answer (?) the last letter of Mr. John Peers by following his example and dis- missing his arguments (?) as being "too childish to be worth a moment's thought," or that of a certain great man who tried to overwhelm those who differed from him re- garding the operation of certain economic principles by saying their opinions were only worthy of the inmates of lunatic asylums; but my so doing would not prove any- thing, unless it were that my claim to "the grand old name of gentleman" was doubtful. "Abuse is not argument," and it may be taken as an axiom in matters of controversy, that when a person resorts to the former, it is because he finds it difficult to support his case by the latter. Mr. Peers has not, therefore, answered my first argument, viz., that loyalty to a common sovereign in an empire like our own is a powerful stimulus to unity and an antidotel to dis- integration. I never said, as he represents me to have said, that the existence of the British Empire depended solely upon this loyalty; but that it was "one of the strongest of the ties of empire" I did say, and it yet remains for him prove the contrary. And as to our not brooking interfer- ence if we determined to alter our constitution, how would it be if we were compelled to brook it It might displease us, we might fight against it, but if the "leaping swords" of our brethren in other climes were to be unsheathed, "the people of England" might have some little difficulty in sheathing them again. And I fail to see is hat right Mr. Peers has to sneer at colonial-loyalty, and to calumnize it as " braggadocia." True there are some natures to whom sentiment is but a name, and who are incapable of being in- fluenced by any of the higher—the heart impulses of humanity; but there are other and nobler natures—chival- ric souls—who think little of fighting, aye, and dying too, for an individual they revere and a system they have learnt . to love. And, perhaps, despite your correspondent's sneers, if occasion required, the "ten thousand leaping swords" would prove to be anything but a myth. And here I may refer to another of his ideas, i.e., that if by some means our constitution were suddenly destroyed, there would not be ten sane men to advocate its restitution. But there might be thousands and even millions of what he considers "in- sane" men (for you have only to disagree with the opinions of a democrat and forthwith you are dubbed a "lunatic ") to advocate its restitution. "Fair traders" have been abundantly stigmatized as " lunatics " of late; but unfor- tunately, judging by Preston, North Lincolnshire and North Durham, the 'lunatics" seem to be in a large majority ; and so it might happen in the event of the sudden change of Government, which Mr. Peers pictures. A great eastern potentate, when in England expressed the astonishment which he had felt in noting the "enthusiasm and affection" with which all classes of Englishmen in all parts of the world spoke of their sovereign. He said, "the other evening you saw the thousands at the Crystal Palace all stand up when the music played the Queen's Hymn. No one tells them to stand; but they stand of their own accord from affection to her. And no wonder, for verily she is the centre of all the glory, all the greatness, and all the prosperity of this grand em- pire." Perhaps a few thousand " lunatics " of this species might be found to advocate the restitution of our monarchi- cal system. And perhaps those who are the owners of "lands, and piles of brick and stone and gold," might not hail the establishment of a republic with enthusiasm; but, On the contrary, feeling that the rights of property were in- secure in the hands of a party with whom modified com- munism is an instinct, perhaps these persons might object to handing over their property to the tender mercies of a republic and be ready even to fight for the grand old con- titution under which the rights of both rich and poor, small I and great, are alike respected. Mr. Peers finds it prudent to slip past arguments number two, three, four, five, and sun- dry ethers, and takes refuge in attacking a sentence or two introduced quite incidentally and by no means indispensable to my case. He disputes the fact that "eclat is lent to great and important national gatherings" by our monarchy. Of course the Volunteer reviews at Windsor and Edinburgh had no eclat lent to them by the presence of royalty; of course the paper which, speaking of the consent of the , Queen to become a patron of one of the most important and I beneficent gatherings of modern times, said that by this patronage the success of the gathering was ensured, did not know what it was talking about; of course the soldier values the Victoria Cross none the more because his sovereign pins It on his breast, and regiments think no more of their colours because she presents them; of course the thousand and one

THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT WITH A POKER AT HUTTON. At the Prescot Police Court, on Friday forenoon, before Meeere, T. Pilkington and W, L. Evans, Edward Ellis, a young man, was brought up on remand charged with having on the previous Sunday night, the 4th inst., at Huyton Quarry, unlawfully wounded his brother, Thomas Ellis, by striking him on the head with a poker.—Superinterident Barker prosecuted, and said that on the night in question the two brothers were drinking together in the Seel Arms public-house, Huyton Quarry, when some angry words passed between them. Prisoner went home before his brother, and when the latter came home the prisoner struck him a severe blow on the head with a poker. The poker was rather a heavy one, and the consequence was that a seriour wound was inflicted.—Thomas Ellis, who appeared in court with a bandage round his head, said: I am a collier, and reside in Wigan-street, Huyton Quarry. Up to Sunday night last I had been lodging at the prisoner's house. That night I and my brother were at the 3eel Arms Inn, and whilst there angry words passed between us, and my brother told me I was not to go to his house any more. My brother left the public-house about half-past nine o'clock, and I left about ten in company with William Jones, who also lodged at the prisoner's house. ';;After leaving the public-house, we stopped a short time on the road talking together, and then went to the prisoner's house. We went round to go in at the back door, but found the yard door was fastened. I tried to open it. I leaned over the door and tried to unbolt it. While I was leaning over the door the prisoner came out of the house and unbolted it. Prisoner said that Jones and his brother could come in, but that I must not enter. I pushed at the door and tried to get in. Whilst I was endeavouring to force my may in, I was struck on the head with some- thing. The blow knocked me down and rendered me sense- less for a short time. The blow cauged a wound on the side of head, and I lost a quantity pf blood. I was taken into a neighbour's house, and Dr. Gorst, who was sent for, dressed the wound. I have been under his care ever since, and have not been able to follow my employment. I don't want to prosecute him, gentlemen. Superin- tendent Barker: I am prosecuting.—Witness : I was the cause of it all.—Superintendent Barker: Stand down.— Witness: I had had drink that night, and tried hard to get into the house. I had no business to push at the door, after I was told that I was not to come.—Superintendent Barker: Did you see what your brother struck you with 2—Witness: No, sir. It was all my fault.—Mr. Pilkington (to prisoner): Have you any questions to ask ?__Prisoner: I wanted to keep him outside the door. (To witness.) I want to know why you did not stop outside the door when I wanted you, and not Coma "interrupting " me ?—Witness: That was my fault.—William Jones deposed: I am a collier, and re- side in Wigan-street, Huyton-Quarry. Up to Sunday night last I lodged at the prisoner's house. On that night I was at the public-house with the prisoner and the last witness. Whilst at the house some angry words passed between the prisoner and his brother. Prisoner left about half-past nine o'clock. I and the last witness remained till ten. After leaving the public-house we went to the prisoner's house. We tried to open the yard door, but found it was fast. The last witness leaned over the door and tried to un- fasten it, but did not do so. The prisoner came out of the house and unfastened it. He unfastened it on the inside.— Superintendent Barker: Did prisoner say anything ?—Wit- ness : Yes. He said, "Who's there ?" and I replied, "It's me." Prisoner then said, "You and your brother can come in."—Superintendent Barker: Did he say anything about the last witness not going in 2—Witness : Yes. He said Thomas (his brother) was not to come —Superintendent Barker: Did Thomas try to get in —Witness : Yes. He was at the door before me.—Superintendent Barker: Whilst Thomas was trying to get in did the prisoner do anything? —Witness: Yes; he struck his brother with a poker. The poker produced is the same.—Mr. Blackwell (assistant - magistrates' clerk): What sort of a blow was it? Thomas was endeavouring to get in, and the prisoner was trying to keep him ont.—Superintendent Barker : Can you say which end of the poker the prisoner had hold of at the time ?—Witness: I can't say. The blow knocked Thomas down, and, for a short time, he appeared to be un- conscious. The blow caused a wound, from which a quantity of blood flowed.—Superintendent Barker: While Thomas was on the ground, did you see the prisoner attempt to strike him a second time ?—Witness ; No; I did not.—Superin- tendent Barker: What distance is the back-yard door from the house door ?__Witness: About four or five yards. LIBERAL RE-UNION AT WARRINGTON. ADDRESS BY MR. J, G. McMINNIES, M.P. A re-union of Liberal members of the Warrington Parlia- mentary Debating Society and their friends took place on Monday evening in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington. Ciansiderable interest was attached to proceedings from the fact that Mr. J. G. MeMinnies, our respected borough member, had consented to preside, and as previous to the close of the last session of the society the Conservative Government had had to resign to make way for a Liberal Administration, the members of the new Liberal "Cabinet" were also expected to be present. About 100 persons sat down to an excellent 'knife and fork tea," the tables being presided over by the following ladies:—Mrs. W. Roberts, Mrs. Holfors, Mrs. Mills' Mrs. H. Rathbone, Mrs. Knowles, and Miss Burrows. Shortly after the proceedings commenced the entrance of Mr. McMinnies caused an outburst of applause, which was renewed on Mr. J. Crosfield and the Speaker of the HO'use " 'making their appearance. The hearty welcome accorded to Mr. McMinnies testified to his popularity, and that, his ser- vices in the House of Commons were appreciated by the Liberal party. Ample justice having been done to the good things provided, the chair was taken by Mr. McMinnies, who was supported on the platform by Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., Mr. F. Monks, J.P., and the Rev. R. Filcher (Premier of the Society), Dr. Huson-More (the Speaker). Amongst those present we noticed, Mr. A. Perris (Chancellor of the Exchequer), Mr. Henry Roberts Home Secretary), Mr. C. J. Holmes (Foreign Secretary), Mr. W. H. Chapman (Colonial Secretary), Mr. W.Roberts (War Secretary), Mr. H. Witham (Indian Secretary), Mr. Thomas Flood (Irish Secretary) Mr. Joseph Gibson (First Lord of Admiralty), Mr. J. Urmson (Post-master General), Mr. A. Rathbone (President of Board of Trade), Mr. G. to do my best for its prosperity. For instance, the seraphic doctor himself, when at Perth, called himself a "Liberal Conservative." (Laughter.) I wonder he I did not go on to describe himself as a triangular circle— (laughter)—he is circular, I knew—(laughter)-4-for I have seen him—(loud laughter and applause)—or a jet black white. But they talk much of Reciprocity, Retaliation, Free Trade, with the "r " turned into the wrong place and called Fair Trade. (Laughter.) Well, sir; you, the gentle- men behind me, and many gentlemen before me, can help us very much in this respect. By your presence in future you can give us very great encouragement, and you can help us by swelling our nutnbers, thereby spreading an increased energy amongst ourselves, and giving us a stimulus for the prosecution of our studies, and the production of the result of those studies in speeches. (Hear, hear.) But I am specially obliged to you, sir, for coming to-night, because I know that after the protracted session which you have gone through, and the heavy arrears of private business which must have been awaiting you, I feel it to be especially good of you to come, and out of the scanty leisure that is afforded to you, give us the benefit of your advice and the encour- agement of your countenance. It is, I feel, a sacrifice which is a real sacrifice on your part—a sacrifice which I must say, on behalf of niyaelf and those I have the honour to act with generally, we appreciate very highly indeed. (Hear, hear.) We are glad also to see other visitors. I trust that, since the calls upon their time are not so press- ing, they *ill favour us in the coming session, now and then at least, if not constantly. I rejoice, sir, in this gathering, that we have you at our head, because in another place our friend the enemy—(laughter)—had his gathering in the shape of a good dinner with an ex-M.P. at the head of the table, and the seraphic doctor I dare say at the tail. (Laughter.) There the seraphic doctor said there were three Prime Ministers present. Thele was the Prime Minister of St. Paul's, the Prime Minister of Trinity, and the Prime Minister of the Debating Society. (Laughter.) He knew, no doubt, as well as I did at that moment, that the gentleman he was speaking of was the Leader of the gpleosition—(hear, hear) —and that we had taken very good care to take the wiud out of their sails before the session ended in order that they might not make capital of their position as "the Govern- ment" during the recess. (Hear, hear.) He told them further, that they were all- three in their prime. The seraphic doctor is fond of that word, for in his address at Perth be says—" I am still in my prime." (Laughter.) Well, perhaps it should Fe forgiven him, because, sir, in an after-dinner speech, even a seraphic doctor is sure to be well primed. (Laughter.) Then, sir, our friend the enemy, in the person of the Leader of the Opposition—of whom, per- sonally, I wish to speak in the highest terms (hear, hear)— said he need not explain the principles of Conservatism, for he felt that they were so well known that he need not ex- patiate upon them. Sir, they may have been well known in that room, but certainly I was a little disappointed that we did not get an exposition of them. I could not help applying to his speech a verse which he applied in another connection— -

"Mee / have been so quickly done for, I wonder what I was began for. (Laughter.) Well, sir, of course, we had the stock phrase about Liberal blundering and plundering. I am surprised that these gentlemen object to plundering," because, sir, if you will look on the 9th of June, 1881, in the paper that is neutral on all questions of politics and religion— (laughter)—you will find the rev, gentleman, announced by the doctor as Prime Minister of Trinity, writes to say that he applauds Lord Beaconsfield in his borrowing the phrase "Men of light and • lead- ing," from Edmund Burke; and of his making a quotation without putting in quotation marks, but does not approve of Mr. Gladstone making a blunder in the "Land o' the leal." "They stand on a very different foot- ing," so I too say, the one was plundering, the other blundering. It seems, however, our friend the enemy can blunder and plunder too. But is it quite true after all that we have been guilty of blundering and plundering? Let me take the Plunders in the Afghan war. Who was it said that war was to cost us five millions? Who was it that made it cost twenty-three or twenty-five millions? (Hear, hear.) Not certainly the Liberals. Either then it was a blunder or it was a lie. (Hear, hear.) Well, then, sir, in regard te "plundering." In 1852 we solemnly recognised the independence of the Boers. In 1877 we annexed their territory. Was it a Liberal Government that piundered on that occasion? We were told, however, by the Conserva- tive Government that the Boers were consenting to that annexation, but when we found such was not the ease we gave them back their liberty. (Applause.) It is made a great point by the Leader of the Opposition that we pro- mised to uphold the Authority of the Queen in the Trans- vaal, and that nothing has happened between that time and this to justify us in not fulfilling that promise. Nothing happened, sir? why, since the Queen's Speech was issued we found out that the alleged consent of the Boers had never been given; we found out that it was a lie; we found out that we had been so utterly misled that we had either to force these people by our arms or give them the justice they demanded. Were we to slaughter thousands to uphold a Conservative lie? They would have done so. They would have had war. They would have hidden their prong in a blaze of glory, and in a deluge of blood. (Uese, hear, and applause.) Of course we had the usual [ging at Mr. Gladstone for his apology to Austria. Those of you who remember the picture in Punch at the time will remember that he drew a cartoon that expressed the truth of the matter very clearly and cleverly that that apology of Mr. Gladstone brought forth a disavowal of the plundering propensities of Austria. Our leader brought forth that disavowal of the plundering propensity on the part of Austria by his simple, speech—" He spake, and it was done." Their leader would have gone to war. The Leader of the Opposition told us that firmness and charity were all that were essential to pacify Ireland. In reply, the Liberal party say justice was needed before charity, for charity is oftimes but 'a salve put on to heal the wounds of outraged justice. (Hear, hear.) He told his followers they must not be caught napping. I can only say we have always found them wide awake, and where " plun- dering" is in the field there is no fear of Tories napping. Of coarse we had the usual talk about empire and freedom, which means, being translated into the tongue " under- standed of the people," the re-establishment of the rule of one which our fathers abolished in 1688, and the freedom for the many to submit to the usurpation and to pay the bill. Then we were informed by the Leader of the Opposi- tion that the Government had not sown its wild oats. We have, however, I believe, sown quite enough wild oats to furnish any amount of Tory chaff. Then the right honour- able gentleman made a statement worthy of the seraphic doctor who really must have sat very close to nrn indeed. He charged the Government with open espousal of the cause of Mr. Bradlaugh. If I were to make any complaint of the Government, if I were to venture to say anything on this occasion, it would be that they did not show themselves firm to their convctions by upholding the principle of which Mr. Bradlaugh happened to be the momentary expression; that owing to the weak-kneed Liberals who thought more of their bigotry and less of their principles—(applause,—the Government was not strong enough to do justice in the face uf the odium attached to the gentleman whose name hap- pened to be for the time being connected with the cause of liberty. (Hear 4 hear.) I sty advisedly that the House of Commons on that occasion dealt a blow to the constitutional liberties of this country which we shall do well to strain every nerve to avenge. (Hear, hear.) Well, sir, such, briefly as I can put them, are our aims, such are our motives, and such our opponents in this debating chamber, and out- side in the glass case near the Post Office to which I have referred. (Laaghter.) It is my aim, and I am sure it is the aim of my friend Mr. Burgess, 49 Leader of the Opposition, to caltivate the utmost courtesy in regard to persons—(hear, hear,)—whilst we practise a sharp and decided' attack and defence for the principles which we severally uphold. (Hear. hear.) I can only say to my friends of the debating society without your aid, and without your encouragement, I can do little or nothing. With your aid—l join bands in this matter with the Leader of the Opposition—with your aid and encouragement I can do very much towards that which I have very much at heart, as I am sure you have very much at heart, viz., to make this society useful and honour- able, a power in the town for instructim and delight. (Loud applause.) Mr. JOHN CROSFIRLD said: I quite agree with the senti- ments of that song, "There's no place like home "—(hear, hear)—and I am afraid in my own case that I carry it rather to too great an extent, perhaps inasnitich as I prefer going home to attending meetings in Warrington when I can help doing so. I have so many to attend of one sort or another that it makes me very glad to go hOme. (Hear, hear.) But, at the same time, I feel that your Prime Minister has read me, along with others, a very sensible lecture to- night—(hear, hear, and applause)—and I can assure him and you that it will afford me pleasure to come to some of your meetings and to listen to some of the arguments on some of the political questions of the day. (Applause.) I have no doubt whatever that I can gain wisdom by doing so , —(hear, hear)—probably more wisdom than if I attended seine of the lectures that are given in the Public flan. (Laughter.) I should like to say that I think we are very much indebted to Mr. Webster for his great kindness in coming down to Lancashire to:teach us men of busiaess how to conduct it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) You know, ladies and gentlemen, I dare say as well as I do, that people who live in London are apt to imagine that they are the whole of England. (Heat., hear.) • I remember getting a letter from a Conservative friend of mine whom I happened to meet abroad some four years ago. In the evening, when we were smoking a cigar together, we got to politics, and once or twice he attempted to attack John Bright, and I attempted John Bright's defence—(hear, hear)—and I need not tell you he got considerably the worst of it. (Loud laughter.) I fancy that this must have rankled in his breast,

because about two years ago I got a letter' which I think filled three sheets of note paper closely written, in which he wrote me a most savage dissertation upon the impolicy of the words which I had. used, and which he had

seen reported in the paper, when Mr. Gladstone went through Warrington. In this letter a which I should I not have mentioned except for this particular expression— he says, " We, in the centre of civilisation." (Loud laughter.) Just that idea that the cockneys have that they are the whole of England. (Laughter.) So I took the liberty when I replied to tell him that if it were not for Lan- cashire and Yorkshire London would go spark out next week. (Loud laughter and applause.) And so I think of my friend Mr. Webster corning here to lecture us on Free Trade or what they call Fair Trade, or Reciprocity or what ever they please to call it. I think that we who live in Lan- cashire are quite capable of judging of that question as well as he Is—(hear, hear)—and I want you just to observe this simple thing that as regards Free Trade the question is, who pays the import duty? The consumer pays the import duty— (hear, hear)—and if you put a ss. duty upon corn at Liver- pool the people in this country pay the duty,—(hear, hear) —not the men across the Atrantic ocean who send it. If I import a case of claret from France I find on my invoice 4s. a dozen charged for duty, and I have to pay it. The men in France who send 'it here do not pay the duty, we who consume it have to pay it. Now you will observe that Mr. Webster never once mentioned the consumer in that lecture of his. (Hear, hear.) Then he talks, you know, as if Old England's trade was going to the dogs, and we might be going to be sold up next month. (Laughter.) I don't like troubling you with figures, hut if you will allow me I will just give you one or two. (Applause.) The real value of exports British aid Irish products and manufactures in 1815 was £51,003,000; in 1849 £51,308,000. They diminished £300,000. In 1859, that was after Free Trade was introducsd into the country, they rose to £130,000,000, and in 1880 they rose to £223,000,000. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Well, the total tonnage of ship- ping belonging to the United Kingdom in 1815 was two millions, and in 1850 was six millions. The fact is this country is progressing at a tremendous speed, and the only way in which they can stop it is by reverting to these crazy Reciprocity, Fair Trade notions. (Hear, hear.) It seems un- necessary for me to say anything about it. I think Lord Derby's speech at Southport—(hear, hear)—is enough to answer anybody, and that admirable, sensible, short letter of John Bright's which you had in the papers this mornine. (Applause.) I think, ladies and gentlemen, Lord Derby and John Bright are quite as eminent authorities as Mr. Webster —(laughter)—and Dr. Mackie. (Applause.) As regards this debating society I think it is of infinite value to the town, especially to the young men,- and I shall take care when my sons leave school—which they will do in a year or two—that they attend this debating class on every occasion they possibly can. (Hear, hear.) I should like to say in passing, looking at this last session of Parliament—in the House of Commons, I don't mean yours—we ought as Liberals to feel extremely indebted to the exertions of the party and our great loader, Mr. Gladstone. (Loud applause.) I think we may rfay without exaggeration that he is the greatest statesman that has lived in this century— (hear, hear, and applause)—and if he never does another stroke of work we, as the Liberal party, must feel indebted to him for the magnificent manner in which he has con- ducted the Liberal party in the House of Commons during the past session. (Hear, 'hear.) We are also indebted to our friend Mr. McMinnies for his conduct—(applause)—and to the whole body of the Liberal party, for the admirable manner in which they have supported Mr. Gladstone during the session. Many Libaal members have restrained ex- pressing their opinions on many occasions for nothing but the desire not to waste the time of the House. (Hear, hear.)

I hope Mr. Gladstone may be spared in health—and that Mr. McMinnies may be spared in health—(he, ar hear)—to con- duct the business of the House of Commons for a good many years to come. (Applause.) I thank you for inviting me here to-night. It is a great pleasure to come, and I wish you every success in the coming session. (Applause.) The Chairman then called upon Mr. ALFRED PERE'S, who said: Mr. Chairman, ladies, and gentlemen,—Every now and vain' weak-kneed Liberals are fain to halt at the bidding of Tory tacticians, who, what- ever else they lack, will never be suspected of wanting assurance that the question may be settled, "Has Liberalism any definite aims?" It is only a short time since I road an article in one of the Conservative organs which stated that Radicalism had landed the Liberal party in hopeless con- fusion, declared that the Whigs were finally dished, and recommended them to take their seats on the back Tory. benches. This kind of remonstrance is calculated to make some of the younger and less reflective amongst us to rub our eyes and ask ourselves whether we should not heed these solemn appeals, and face our political responsibilities afresh. Has Liberalism any definite aims, and if so what are they ? One of the difficulties attending this inquiry arises from the fact that political history cannot be taught in a few. lessons. Liberal thought must be retrospective as well as viewy. It strikes its roots into the vast. If it did not there could be

little promise in it. The Liberal leaders of to-day are not the less in the line of apostolical succession because their vision has widened, because the vast accumulation of modern fact has caused a corresponding expansion of the political horizon. They are inspired by, great examples. They claim kindred with noble souls who 'fought the battles of freedom when the same or similar forces of prerogative and privilege were arrayed against them, as now confront the political reformer. It would be amusing if it were not at the same time sad to hear bigots and reactionary alarmists quote great Englishmen in favour of measures, which if they were now alive, they would scorn and oppose. These peo- ple have never laid hold of that principle which binds all nature together throughout her evolving series, and runs like a golden thread through all the acts and stages of human history.—the Law of Growth, conditioning and rendering the gam secure—which are the outcome of struggle and the fruit of experience. I can only place on record my own con- viction, which must be taken for what it is worth, that the im- partial study of English constitutional history never yet made a man amore enthusiastic Tory, but has manyatime made a mana more intelligent and confirmed Liberal. (Applause.) It is, however, hopeless to expect that the great mass of the Hy. ing generation, who, for the most part, have lacked the new privilege of impartial instruction, and to a wide extent have been in the hands of the Society for the Promotion of Political Ignorance, can ever be entirely self-taught in political science. (Applause.) ' Like the French peasantry, who are naturally intelligent, they know very little of their own history, but they know quite enough to be satisfied that they cannot rest content with the items and scraps and pompous phrases which are doled out to them by an interested clerical caste. They are awake and ask for food which shall nourish their growing needs. They appreciate the humblest attempt to lay before them the new problems in the light of old facts. Had time permitted I should like to have run over the category of ,Liberal aims on this occasion, bet I can do no more than mention one or two of the leading points. The fundamental principle of all Liberal action is universality of freedom. Civil and religious liberty the wide world over is a sentiment which always flows gracefully from the lips of the orator. It will not bear exposition. If it ho not a mere phrase, a bit of political cant, it must be connected with accomplished facts in the putt, and definite ideals in the future. (Applause.) The revolution of MSS was precipitated by acts of tyranny on the part of the Crown, and those who brought it about fostered the hopes and aspirations which bore fruit in the age which followed. The social and civil liberties were laid broad and deep in those troublesome times. In later days, when the colonies revolted against unnatural restraint and oppressive taxation, the Whigs, with Burke as their leader, raised a voice of sublime protest against govern- ment which was contrary to the interest of the goverued. (Hear, hear.) From the days of Milton until quite recently the complete emancipation of the press has had to be carried on against fearful odds and against great personal loss and risk in many cases. (Hear, hear.) The liberation of slaves in British dominions is within the memory of living men, and it is but a few years ago that we heard a cry sent forth from this town of Warrington against a circular-letter issued by a Conservative Government which provided for the surrender of refugees by captains in the British Navy. The claims of Slav and Greek would have been unheard for another generation if Conservative convenience and inertia had notbeen broken in upon by the vigilantlovers of human freedom in the ranks of Liberalism. (Applause.), Bulgaria and Montenegro and other oppressed nationalities, have to thank a Tory Government it is true, but it is for their unparalleled stupidity which providentially sealed the doom of the rotten despotism it was so concerned to favour and defend. (Applause.) The liberty of religious associat,ion is not at all an ancient privilege, and every school-boy ought to know that it was gained for us, piece by piece' wrung from unwilling hands by rue champions of the good cause. So also the Test Acts which excluded Dissenters from civil offices, and the Catholic Disabilities, which denied the right of full citizen- ship to many thousands of our fellow countrymen, were swept away in the teeth of the bitterest Tory opposition. That this should be borne in mind by our Catholic friends when called upon to exercise the franchise I need hardly point out. (Applause.) The freedom of commerce was secured after a long and arduous struggle, in which it was abundantly shown that there were Englishmen then who could prove themselves so unworthy of their ancestry as to desire the continuance of a state of things which condemned the masses of the community to chronic poverty and serfdom. The movements which have culminated in granting the right of combination to the labourers equally with the capitalist class, also met with similar opposition from Con- servative politicians. The endowed schools of the country would still have been the preserves of the clergy, and the universities have been closed to the conscientious objectors to false swearing, had not the advocates of free thought and speech taken those venerable bulwarks of bigotry by assault. (Applause.)' But time would fail me to tell of Liberal triumphs in freedom's sacred cause, (Applause.) The achievem eats of the Liberal party are but an earnest of others that have yet to come. The recognition of the law of progress ranks next in the order of Liberal aims, but upon this I cannot dwell. It is a matter of fact and observation that the Mrces which are arrayed against great measures, and whim, unite Liberals together in a common cause, are usually reactionary ones. The timid, the lovers of antiquated privilege and tradition, those who cling to the symbols of vanisniog Feudalism are usually to he found in the Tory camp. Haters of science, tretnblers at the advance of critical thought, those who love darkness rather than light, usually find an easy refuge there. In the Liberal roll there are great names which are the watchwords of the f uture—Richard Cobden—(applause)— the organiser of commercial treaties, and ,vleiaavlel cheapened food for the people and enriched 11 John Bright, the eloquent apostle of Free Trade; and far transcending every name that has ever Lo men-

tipned in the Liberal roll, William Ewart Gladstone—(loud ebeers)—the prophet statesman, whose varied gifts have been poured out unsparingly in the Liberal cause. (Ap- plause.) Could Toryism hold such a soul? (No.) Nay, verily, it has had enough to retain a chivalrous nature like that of Lord Carnarvon as it has been unable to held a clear-headed statesman like Lord Derby. (Applause.) • But if you look for whole-hearted conviction, for passionate aspiration after attainable, but still unattained good, for steady perseverance in the pursuit of great objects and a keen insight into the possibilities of legislative action, if you desiderate free play of the imagination and far-seeing anticipation of the needs which a still youthful and vigorous nationality manifests during its growth, you nmst:expeet to find them in the van of that movement which takes the law of progress for its guiding light, which asks not, first, what is convenient, and secondly, what is true; but asks first, what is right, and then only how can the true be made the convenient. (Applause.) The Cnermarax, in introducing Dr. Hnson-More to the audience, said one of the worst fates which could befall a member of Parliament was to be named by the Speaker. There was a tale told that in the time of the younger Pitt the House was very disorderly, and the Speaker called out "Order, order," until he was quite tired. At last he said " Gelatle- men, if hon. members do not keep order I shalt have to name names;" and Pitt, crho was a member at that time, addressed the Speaker and said, "What would happen if you did name me?" and the Speaker replied, "God alone knows." (Laughter.) %. He was going to do what no mem- ber of the House of Commons could do—name the Speaker —(laughter)—and call upon him to address them. That was what the Speaker of the House of Commons never did, but he is called the Speaker because he never speaks. (Laughter and applause). Dr. HusoN-Ilionit (the Speaker) said: Mr. Chairman ladies and gentlemen, I have heard to-night a number of political remarks from very able speakers. Now, although the Speaker, as Mr. McMinnies has just said, I don't often speak. Good as parliamentary debating societies are in training young men to speak, and men perhaps not still quite young, the only one who is left out in the cold, and who has not much chance of being trained to speak, is the Speaker. I have watched through the past session numbers of gentlemen on both sides of me and in front of me im- L proving visibly and andibl7 in their manner of speaking, and more clearly arranging their thoughts. I have had to it unable to do that, at all events, to practice. If, therefore, I should be unable to repress any of my natural timidity and shyness, and it shows forth, I shall run behind Mr. Filcher for protection. (Laughter and applause.) However, I was pleased to 'hear from the lips of our Chairman that our success during the past ses- sion had been such that there was very much in our practices that could with advantage be borrowed by an assembly in another place. (Hear, hear.) I think so too. (Hear, hear.) Amongst other things referred to pertaining to matters of debate was the accommodation they gave to ladies in this other place. I know that we do better than that; we do not put them in a cage; we put them in the highest place where they can get and where we can see them. And instead of them doing as has been suggested would be the case in the House of Commons—cause mem- bers to neglect their duties,—l believe it stimulated many of our members very keenly indeed, to speak clearly and to express themselves more intelligibly. (Hear, hear.) Other- wise they might have kept quiet. I don't purpose speaking politically because my very office makerrme neutral. lam a neutral colour. (Laughter.) [He was dressed inn suit of grey.] I am what I might call a political bat; I don't belong to either party. I have to keep the ball rolling, amicably, if possible. If it rolls in any other way we at once stop. So that the bat applies in two or three ways. Mr. McMinnies, by the way, a little while ago, asked that everybody in the room and their friends who were not already members to become members. It is true the society has pot any rule prohibit- ing ladies as members, but I may remark that the ladies of Warrington are trying to out-do us altogether by having a society of their own If they do Lehould recommend the gentlemen of Warrington to look to their laurels; they will then require hearts of oak and to be always ready. (Hdr, hear.) There is a matter referred to by Mr. Filcher of great moment in connection with this society, and which it Is especially my duty to look after—the maintenance of absolute courtesy during debate. (Hear, hear.) Na matter how heated anyone may get; no matter how earnestly he may feel the force of the arguments he is employing, he I must never forget to be a gentleman, and whatever may be said from one side to the other, must always be taken as being "opinion. Personalities, officially, are not permitted, and it were well if that duty of the speaker were to fall in abeyance from disuse or from not being needed. I would therefore strongly support Mr. Pilcher's request that a strict courtesy be adhered to. (Hear, hear.) The uses of Parliamentary Debating Societies have been referred to over and over again to-night. One thing that has not been mentioned, not been thought of possibly, is that in these debating societies, however impossible it was in the ordinary debating clubs and young men's improvement societies, ' matters of ordinary moment can be got through rapidly from thsre being practical rules of conduct. Subjects of very great interest and great importance are thoroughly thrashed out by being thrown from one side to the other. The truth, therefore, must necessarily come out, and every man who saw the truth must of necessity become more Liberal-minded. (Hear, hear.). It cannot be helped. (No.) If you see anyone becoming more Liberal-minded drive a truth at them. That we shall have a good session in the one coming I sincerely treat, and that our nninbera shall be so hire) that we shall be obliged to ask the Co-operative Society to enlarge the roof or enlarge the boundary of the room. Last session we had enough room and to spare, but nest session I hope that we shall have so many more mem- bers that we shall have to appropriate the Guardian office to our own use. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. FRET) Molars next addressed the meeting. He said: Ladies and gentlemen, I am afraid the evening is far spent, and we have bad a good deal said that will require thinking about. There is but little left for me to speak about, but I will just say a few words upon the practical application of the principles of which we have just heard. First of all let me thank the members of the society for their invitation to be present to-night. One of the uses of the society looked at from a practical point of view, is that it aids the Liberal party in this borough to fight elections which are necessary, and is a great aid to the spreading of Liberal principles. If we have in Warrington to fight the battle of Liberalism we require, and shall need, all the help we can get besides the mere spending of money. If there is one thing more than another that is calculated to bring Liberal- ism and Conservatism into disrepute it is that abominable practice of bribery, which is prevalent in electioneering times. If I thought that the Liberal party of Warrington had to figlit by such means, and so to win their elections, I don't hesitate to say that I would semr my connection from it; and, therefore, I regard such a society as the one which you are encouraging to-night as a powerful influence in the borough for sweetening party cooegti and helping party victories in a legitimate and honourable way. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Then there is another thing which has been referred to, and which I thoroughly endorse and which as Liberals we are not, I think, sufficiently careful to culti- vate. I was very glad to hear your Speaker refer to that subject, and to say that it is his object and aim to con- duct the society in such a way that all the members shall conduct themselves as gent'emen one to another. One of the things we have to learn as Liberals is that of toleration of differences of opinion between each other. I fully believe that the Conservatives from their point of view as honestly consider that they are in the right as we, and after all seeing that it is a matter of opinion to a large extent, and smatter of intelligent observation, I think that the Liberal party will gain more largely by that toleration' thinking that others may be as honest aa ourselves, and differ entirely from us. (Applause.) I think I have seen in one or two debates that I have attended that disposition, and I am quite sure that it is the aim ef your Prime Minister that you shall recognise such differences, and think none the worse of a man because he happens to differ with you. If we as Liberals feel so strong in our position, as I believe we have a right to do, we shall not lose anything by free and fair discussion upon the question. (Hear, hear.) div.head: "TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: "TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
BY A SOUTII-YVEST_LANCASICRE GENTLEMAN.

[SPEct are] No. XVI. BETHLEHEM. • It was no email pain to us to have to drop Hebron out of our plan. Hebron, the long cherished home, and final rest- ing place of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; the home from which the patriarchal family went down into Egypt; oae of eitiee of refuge; the scene of David's early reign over Judah, and of Absalom's revolt against his reign in Jerusalem over all Israel. Who would not desire to see Hebron? Who would not wish to sit at the door of a tent on the plain of Mamre? Yet the journey there and bock, which the pro- gramme required to be done in one day, was represented as so arduous for one day's ride, that we reluctantly consented to make Bethlehem and the Pool of Solomon our boundary line to the south, and to take these as a day's excursion from Jerusalem. When I consider the effect of the whole journey upon two or three of our party, the utter exhaus- tion they experienced before reaching Beyrout, I think the resolve to spare ourselves at the beginning was a wise and fortunate one, however much we may regret the loss we sustained. It was on Wednesday, the 15th of March, we visited Bethlehem. A day of more real enjoyment I have seldom spent. We had to snake final choice of our ponies for the entire journey before we started. It was my lot to have two taken from me, with which I was tolerably well pleased, before I got astride of the patient steady beast that bore me over Palestine and Syria. I cannot say h for the appearance of my Arab steed. Mrs. Heman's apostrophe to one of his brethren "My beautiful! my beautiful !" would scarcely have fitted poor " Jericho," although he coil I oeten have put in a full claim to the other half of the line "that standest meekly by." Of course we must say nothing of his" proudly arched and glossy neck and dark fiery eye." But never mind poor Jericho ! I have in grateful recollection all thy patient toil, thy scrambles, wet with sweat, up rocky mountain sides, thy cautious tread down rugged tracks, and, then on smoother paths, thy gentle, easy trot. Fine, graceful, even fiery steeds were in the cavalcade, but none was more beautiful than thou wert in my eyes before I bade thee "good bye" on the shores of the great sea. Poor Jericho! (I hit upon the name in entire ignorance of Mark Twain having dubbed his ear- scratching, lean, limping, but, I fear, after all, somewhat libelled, beast by the same patronymic.) Poor Jericho had one antipathy; he had a mortal dislike to Mr. Marsden's " Grinning Bobby." Bobby was a slight made chestnut pony, always on an ambling trot, and always showing his teeth. Jericho knew at once when Bobby was behind, and would either move to one side to let him pass, or put on a brisker step to get out of his way. Dr. Verco had a white pony, very nice to look at, very, his tail was dyed orange colour—they are very fond of bright colours in the east, as my readers may imagine--but he was very uneasy to ride— " all is not gold that glitters "—and his rider was very glad when be was half-way over Palestine to exchange him for a sober mule on whose back he could lie full length. Then Mr. Black had a brown horse not unlike Jericho, but less beautiful ; scraggy but rather brisk •, always ready for a race, and, in this respect, admirably and unfailingly in the spirit of his master. But this is a sad digression. We left our tents for Bethlehem at half-past nine am., and, after travelling about two miles our way lay through a beautiful country. The road, though un- usually level for Palestine' runs between hills of consider- able magnitude, the more distant ones to the right being covered with the dark rich olives and showing some fine specimens of terrace cultivation by which their fruitfulness is carried to their very summit. Several villa residences adorn the hill-sides, giving evidence of far more than Moslem industry and neatness. The land, it seems, is to a great extent in the hands of German colonists, to whose superior management it is indebted for a richer beauty and luxuriance than prevail in most of the other parts of Pales- tine. About a mile from Bethlehem is the tomb of Rachel, a small mosque-like structure, which, I suppose, it is quite certain covers her dust. Poor Rachel! with all her womanly weaknesses, but wifely worth, how greatly she has been honoured above all the queens of earth in having her place of sepulchre preserved for thirty centuries to awaken the love and confirm the faith of the devout from all lands. At a considerable distance from Bethlehem we saw the village standing out on the side of the hill, its white houses shin- ing in the rays of the sun. It occupies a ridge which shoots out from the mountain chain towards the east, and drops down abruptly into the valleys; the slopes being beautifully terraced round the ridge on which the village stands. As we passed under its arched gateways and nar- row streets, I felt more pleased with Bethlehem than with any place we had yet seen in the East. It has an air of busy life, and is evidently undergoing enlargement and improvement. The men are more active, the women more fresh and beautiful, the houses better built, and the streets, upon the whole, more open and cleanly than in any other town or village in Palestine. I have no doubt the secret of all this is, that the Mahommedan population is a mere unit, and that the Christians, so-called, have chief possession and control of the town. Of course the latter have also possession of all the apocryphal sites and relics in Bethlehem which are crowded together in the Church of the Nativity, just as they are in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem. I shall not weary and offend my readers by dwelling upon the various things we saw within the walls of this celebrated church, such as the very spot on which the Saviour was born; the manger in which He was laid, manufactured of brown and white marble; the place on which the Magi paid their adoration, etc., etc., etc. Here also the Greek, Latin, and Armenian churches strive for pre-eminence—the Greeks always securing it. Leaving them to strive and struggle, let us pass into the open square and breathe the pure air of heaven. It is market day; in close proximity to the church are spread heaps of fruit and grain, surrounded by varied busy groups. Looking from this fine esplanade, which is a part of the mountain ride on which the town is seated, we see a succession of mountains covered with their thick foliage of olive and fig trees, and beyond there the dreary, barren wilderness of Judea stretching away to the Dead Sea with its rugged fringe of slaty bills. Immediately below the town, as we look from the edge of the esplanade, is a small plain or valley in which it is supposed the shepherds were watching their flocks when the angels came down. I have a feeling that this valley is too near the town for the event to have occurred there. The long valley on the other side of the hill, as it were to the back of the town, and which stretches through a beautiful range of hills towards the Pools of Solomon, appears to me to be much more likely, because a much more retired, situa- tion. Referring to a letter I wrote home the same evening, I find the following reflections:—" It has been a gladsome day to stand within the town of David, and within sight of the plains and mountains on which the ruddy stripling fed his father's flocks,' where also the angels descended to an- nounce the tidings of great joy—the tidings that within a few yards of the place where these my feet have trod to-day, the Son of the living God had assumed our mortal flesh. It is almost too much to think of. I thought, as I came alone.; of the wise men pursuing this very path, after their inter- view with Herod, and of the moving star that guided them all the way; I thought, too, of the lowly parents making their way in the opposite direction to present the Divine child in the Lord's house at Jerusalem; of Herod's myr- midons, with their slaughter weapons, going forth to fill Bethlehem and its coast with blood and wailing. Surrounded by all these sac-ed scenes and associations one seems to be moving in a long and ever-changing day-dream, and the passing wonder is how we happen to find ourselves so far from home traversing this wonderful land over which, in imagination, we have often in our lifetime trod." POOLS OF SOLOMON.

One hour's ride from Bethlehem, along the bed of an old narrow aqueduct, which once supplied Bethlehem and Jeru- salem with water, brought us to the Pools of Solomon. The mountain scenery on both sides of this track is of the most varied and pleasing character, the only drawback being the never-ending obtrusiveness of loose white stones scattered over the mountain sides, where once the creeping vine, the • spreading fig-tree, aud the feathery olive clothed them with perennial beauty. Even now, despite all the evi- dences of neglect and consequent desolation, and all the marks of Divine displeasure that reign through this once favoured land, the smile of the beneficent Creator I still lingers over it in the exquisite flowers which every- where bedeck its patches of green sod, and which, in some of its richer deposits, shine out a perfect blaze of beauty. The Pools of Solomon are three in number—splendid reservoirs, , one running into the other, I suppose, originally for filtering purposes, the lowest one being connected with the aqueduct over which we travelled. Great was the croaking of the giant frogs in the upper pool as we sat at lunch in their immediate vicinity, and under the shadow of a castle built as a protection against the in- cursions of the Bedouin Arabs in the seventh century. Close to the to of the upper pool is a splendid spring, of water. You may stand at the mouth of the deep well and hear its incessant dash at the bottom as it rushes from the mountain side into the water courses which, I believe, still convey it -co Bethlehem On our return ride to Jerusalem we were in- creasingly impressed with the beauty and fertility of the land around Bethlehem. The road being quite level after we passed the tomb of Rachel, our more impetuous horsemen according to their wont, rode quickly forward—indeed, had, a good race, leaving a cloud of dust behind, and also poor Jerry and me, to find our way alone, indulging in such mediations as the journey and our mutual state of mind in; Spired. Jerry's long easy step made me always feel he was favourable to the exercise. The next day was spent in mak- ing our final purchases of olive-wood souvenirs, dried flowers, etc., and Friday morning, March 17, saw our tents lifted amid all the noise and confusion inseparable from manipulation. But when we consider all they had to do and the short time they had to do it in, not only on this morning, but every morn- ing when we were on the move, the wonder is how .the work was done at all. Only think! About seventy horses and mules to be saddled or loaded with tents, trunks, and nepots,alpans, beds and bedding, bags and baggage, all kinds, the horses meekly waiting for us to mount, and of a the mules, each with a bell to its bridle, patiently steadying themselves while the muleteers were hauling and screaming as they strapped the various packages over their thickly- padded backs. A lively scene was our tenting-ground every morning, with seventy beasts and thirty or forty men to attend upon a party of seventeen. Leaving them in the thick of the turmoil we rode round the north-east corner of the city, and down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, en route to Jericho. As we ascended the Mount of Olives, we turned again and again to take a last lingering look at the old city,

o "beautiful for situation," And once "the joy of the whole earth." Farewell, city Of God! Thou only spot of earth on which the rays of glory from the throne of the Eternal pouted forages directly down! City of Perdition ! over whose stones, as well as. people, the tears of Omnipo- tence were shed, and whose soil, saturated with the blood of martyrs, opened its mouth, and, in return for all His pity- ing love, drank M the blood of God's own Son! Oh, I Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who can withhold a tear when he I thinks of thine unparalleled privileges, thy fearful perversity, thine unspeakable woes! (To be continued next week.)

Dr. Verco, writing to a friend from "The camp out- , side Jerusalem" says : On the way to Jerusalem I we passed through the valley of Aijalon and had lunch ; saw Kirgath-jearim stuck on a bill, where the ark rested for twenty years. Saw Mizpeh in the distance, and Gibeon, and Emmaus; crossed the brook from which David chose the five smooth stones, one of which was too much for Goliath; had a good deal of up and down riling among the hills of Judea, and reached Jerusalem about four o'clock. As the hotels were all full we had to camp out. Our tents were all arranged and looked very clean and nice. We were stiff enough and sore enough, and glad to get on our feet again. That night we did have a night. Though as tired as a dog, I could not get a wink of sleep till four o'clock for there was a perfect tempest abroad. The wind howled through the trees, and rattled the tents and strained the pegs, and bumped the bed, till I thought the whole machine was com- ing to the ground. However, it fortunately lasted the night through, but in the morning, while I was writing, the wind- ward side collapsed and came down about my ears. It rained too, so the major part of us were transferred to three rooms in a house close by, where we have been ever since. Hence I can scarcely say how I appreciate camping out. Our meals we all have in a tent called the "Grand Saloon." We sit with our bats and caps on, and sometimes our over- coats and mackintoshes, so that we form a queer dinner group. We have each a small iron bedstead and nice clean clothes, table, and cloth, candle, basins, jugs, towels, &c. Tur- key rugs on the floor, so that we are not at all uncomfortable. There is another tent, the cooking galley. There is no stove, bat a couple of small iron troughs in which charcoal is burned, and on which are set all the pots and kettles. The food isn't bad, but it doesn't come up to the hotels; it cannot be expected to be, mixed and tended and served by Arabs, and besides, coming in through the cold winds, the food gets extremely cold. But we enjoy it because we have such insatiable appetites. We have seen the places of interest in and about Jerusalem, and a day's walk certainly gives one a better idea of the sur- roundings of the city than any books could possibly do. On Sunday we went to the Mount of Olives, and Bethany, and came home along the Jericho-road that by which the Saviour entered the city in triumph. We have been to the pool of Siloam and the pool of Gibron, and the field of blood, to the tombs of the judges, and the tombs of the kings. The things or places that have most pleased and impressed me are the mount of Olives, the pool of Bethesda. Mount Moriah was not quite large enough to build the temple with its large area upon. To-day I have had a new horse brought for my approval, and I think he will be far easier than the other, though he is not quite so young or strong. Two gentlemen intend going the journey in palanquins, a sort of box, borne between two mules, one in front, one behind. What a sight we shall be. One is an old gentleman, very shaky, who couldn't endure the horse-riding—the other a nearly blind young man, who cannot see to guide a horse. Truth to tell, we are rather an odd lot, though I suppose about as respectable as most. Said old parson is very shaky. Another who looks like a chip a century old, or a dried-up mummy, is almost as deaf as a post, and puts a great silver bell to his ear and shouts " What's that?" A third, young White- head, is almost deaf, and nearly blind. A fourth has a head which is always on the wriggle, and a wife about 30 years his junior, a Quakeress, and fat, and a couple of eyes that look outwards at the same thing; so that whether she is looking at the mount of Olives, or the field of blood, or at the uttermost parts of the earth, it is difficult to decide. But he's a dear old fellow nevertheless, and his wife, though a Quakeress, the jolliest woman of the company. She wears specs., and so of necessity sits up straight, and holds her head well up. The couple are very loving, and total ab- stainers to the back bone. I don't know whether or not they have decided to go the whole journey. We picked this couple up at Port Said. We very nearly picked up Philip Phillips, the singing pilgrim. He sat next to me at dinner at Port Said, and said he would wait for us at Joppa, and come along with us, but in conaquence of our delay and his engagements at Jerusalem he had to go on ahead of us.

W. Hazlehurst. MARRYING IN HASTE AND REPENTING AT LEISURE.— Walter Tweedale (30), plasterer, was charged under a war- rant, by the Runcorn Board of Guardians, with leaving his wife chargeable to the common fund of the union, on the 3rd July.—Mr. W. H. Linaker watched the case on behalf of the Guardians, and Mr. Burton appeared for the defence. —Mr. Peter Wright, relieving officer, said the prisoner's wife became chargeable to the union on the 9th ult. She made application to him, saying that her husband had left her without shelter or anything to eat, and she had to apply to her parents for food and lodging. She appeared before the Guardians, and they admitted her into the workhouse. Tweedale went away, and was afterwards found working near Edge Hill. She had now been in the house five weeks, and her maintenance had, probably, cost about 4s. per week. —Mr. John Armstrong, 17, Brunswick-street, said he was the father of the young woman, who was 17 years of age. They were married last year, and lived together up to June, in Surrey-street. His daughter then came to him and told him they had quarrelled on several occasions. He replied that they must make matters up between themselves, as he did not wish to interfere, and always had an excellent opinion of the prisoner. One day, some short time afterwards, the young man locked up the house and went off to his parents at Acton Bridge.—Mr. Burton said the marriage had been an early and imprudent one. Complainant had frequently reproached her husband with "not being the right one for her," and had said there was another man she ought to have had, and she would have the bailiffs in some day and sell the furniture. Eventually she left, saying she should not return, and the prisoner then sent his furniture away to a place of safety. He had been employed by the railway com- pany, and earned 18s. per week, but whilst at Bootle lately he had suffered from an attack of rheumatic fever, and being kept from his work a month. He was willing to allow his wife a reasonable sum per week. Perhaps as the couple grew older they would decide to bear with one another's weak- nesses, but at present the young man refused to resume co- habitation.—Prisoner agreed to allow his wife 4s. per week, and pay the 18s. owing for maintenance, and ss. casts; and he was then discharged. ONE WHO OUGHT TO SIGN THE PLEDGE. Joseph Bell, a boat captain, was charged with having been drunk on the licensed premises known as the Swan inn, and kept by a man named Ogden.—lnspector Honing- worth said that about half-past ten on the night of the 10th August, he visited the Swan Inn, in company with Sergeant Walley. He found defendant sitting in a room on the left hand side of the door, with some beer before him, and drunk. He spoke to the landlord, who told Bell to drink his beer and leave.—Sergeant Walley gave corroborative evidence, and P.D. Noden was also called to support the statements of the other officers as to defendant's conduct in the street, which clearly proved he was under the influence of liquor. —Defendant denied that he had any drink in the house, and said his conduct in the street, which the officers had spoken of as supporting their statement that he was drunk, arose owing to his having been struck on the mouth by a man who was passing.—He called Mrs. Pettifer, mother-in-law of the landlady of the house' who said defendant was not sup- plied with any beer; and his wife, who stated that there had certainly been a quarrel between her and her husband in the house, owing to his having been on the spree some days be- fore, and trying to sell his horse—At this point defendant made some remarks which caused the Chairman to say that he appeared to be under the influence of drink even then. —Bell answered that he had not taken any for weeks.—The Chairman said he was glad to hear it, and he hoped de- fendant would never touch it again. He had, however, to remind him that there were eight previous convictions against him, all of which were apparently caused through taking liquor. He would be fined ss. and 235. costs, and, in default of payment, have to suffer 14 days' imprisonment.— Defendant's wife paid the money, and narrowly escaped being locked up whilst doing so, owing to the strong lan- guage in which she gave relief to her overburdened feelings. A WEsx CASE.—Thomas Wood was charged, on remand, with stealing 841bs. of rope, the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Co.—James Weedall, dock constable, gave evi- dence to the effect that he found the ropes produced in the possession of the prisoner. On questioning him he said that some of themhad been purchased by him from a man in Widnes, who was taking them to a marine store; and the hauling line produced be found in the canal.—Mr. Joseph Littler identified the ropes as the property of the prosecu- tors by a red strand which runs through the middle of each one. The cmpany did not sell ropes in small amounts.— Mr. Lake defended the prisoner, and contended that there was not the slightest evidence against him. There was nothing to show that he had not brought the ropes.—The Bench discharged the prisoner on the ground of there not being sufficient evidence to convict.

div.p: GOLBORNE.

AT'TEMPTING TO UPSET A TRAIN.—On Saturday, at the Newton Police Court, two lads, named Walter Files (14) and Wm. Wedley (15), were charged with placing two pieces of wood on the London and North-Western Railway at Golborne, with intent to obstruct the engine and carriages travelling thereon. The lads, who pleaded guilty, on Sun- day, the 28th tilt., were seen to place the obstruction named across the rails by a publican named George Bradley, who had them removed about half a minute before a passenger train to Wigan passed. The defendants had gone on to a bridge to see the effects of their freak, which Mr. Preston, \ the prosecuting solicitor, said might have been disastrous.— The Bench inflicted a fine of 20s. and costs, or one month, and regretted that on account of their age they could not order the lads to be whipped.

FARNWORTH AGRICULTURAL SHOW. • The seventeenth annual exhibition of this society was held yesterday, at Farnworth, in charming weather. The show field is the commodious one used by the committee of the Widnes Athletic Sports, and is one of the finest of its kind in the county for the particular purpose. The usual custom has been to only devote one day to the exhibition, but this year the committee decided to carry it over two days, in order to give the working-classes a proper oppor- tunity of attending. No doubt the financial result, should the weather prove as lovely to-day (Saturday), as it was yesterday, will prove this to have been a prudent resolve. It is now some years since the society commenced its opera- tions, under somewhat discouraging circumstances, and it is only through the indefatigable exertions of a committee of gentlemen, acting in conjunction with Mr. Robert Whalley, the veteran farmer, that it has reached the present good position which it at present occupies. There is not the slightest doubt that its existence has had a capital effect in improving agriculture, by exciting a commendable emula- tion amongst the farmers. The general public would scarcely suppose that within a few miles of the smoke and alkali vapours of the much-criticised town of Widnes, are to be found some first rate farms, of which that possessed by Mr. Whalley may be cited as an example. The society corn- prizes within its limits Bold, Burtonwood, Cronton, Cuerdley, Ditton, Eccleston, Garston, Hale, Halewood, Huy- ton, Penketh, Prescot, Rainhill, Roby, Sankey, Speke, St. Helens, Sutton, Tarbock, Warrington, Whiston, Widnes, Woolton, and Little Wooltou.
