(Hear, hear.) The county representatives had done all they could in support of Sir Wm. Harcourt's (the member for Oxfordshire) proposed amendment to the Act of 1878, with the object of altering the ptesent method of chargine• the maintenance of main roads principally upon the farming class. On this matter the Conservatives were very nearly successful in defeating the present strong Government. However, he did not intend to talk politics that day, or to say one word which would offend any one present; but though they had no doubt different political opinions, there was one thing upon which they were unanimous, and that was in having at heart the maintenance of that good feeling which he knew had always existed between the landlord, the tenant, and the labouring man. He thought material relief might be given to farmers by following out the scheme which Vernon Varcourt had proposed. Colonel Blackturne next paid a high compliment to his distinguished colleague, Sir R. A. Cross, whose merits and anxiety to serve them they all knew very well; but he remarked that he.would not yield to thg right hoe. gentleman in the matter of his own anxiety to do his duty to the great constituency which had returned him to Parliament. (Hear, hear). He was one of their county representatives, and so long as he had that honour he looked upon himself as bound to look After their individual interests, no matter what might be the par- ticular political opinions which they held. So lone.' as he had the honour of their confidence, he would do his duty by them and put forth every endeavour to serve them. He had been asked to propose the toast of "The Farnworth Agricul- tural Society," and he did so with the greatest pleasure. (Applause). As a landlord and a neighbour to that place, he had long felt the greatest interest in the operations of the society. He had for years been a supporter of it, as was his father before him, who used to attend its meetings up to the last year of his life, and always looked forward with interest to its exhibition. When he (the speaker) left home on Tuesday to go to Bolton and other places, he told his farm bailiff to allow all the men to attend the show that day. Seventeen years had gone since the society was first established, and he was of opinion that such organisations were of the greatest advantage to the community. On such occasions as that the farmers compared notes. In conclu- sion, all he could say was that so long as be remained a resident in that part of the country—and he hoped to do so up to the end of hie career—he should be found a staunch supporter of the organisation. (Loud applause.) Mr. WHALLEY who was called upon to respond, said that he could say that he hoped, with all his heart, that the wish of Colonel Blaekburne as to continuing his connection with the society might be realised. He next referred to the ex- cellent results which had sprung from such societies, but he was persuaded that they had been more beneficial to the landlord than the tenant farmer. That society had been better supported by the manufacturers of the district than by the landlords, and, indeed, it would not have been what it was that day but for the manufac- turers. Good times for farmers were the best time for landlords. Going round the country, he came to the conclusion that "the land was going down ;" it was not in the sound condition as it was years ago, as the farmers had lived upon it too long. He, for one, found it was a very bad thing to live upon the land. He would be bound to say, taking Lancashire and Cheshire through, that one half of the farmers were insolvent. Indeed, On Tuesday, he was told by a very large dealer in corn, who was also a farmer, that his statement was not correct, as not one-third of there were solvent. In conclusion, he proposed the health of Sir A. B. Walker, president of the society. (A pplanse.) The toast was drunk with musical honours, after which the CHAIRMAN suitably replied, and gave "The Judges," which was acknowledged by Mr. Joint SCOTSON. The CHAIRMAN called upon a Mr. Mackie, of Warrington, who in the course of his remarks spoke in very flattering terms of Colonel Blackburne. He made some observations of a sneering character concerning Mr. John Btight's ex- planation of the depressed condition of the country being attributable to want of sunshine, and hinted that seine years ago the explanation offered by the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster as to the dull trade was a different one ! The proceedings at the luncheon then terminated. I The show will be continued to-day (Saturday). PRIZE LIST. SACItILEGE IN CHESIIIII.E.--At the Northwich Police Court, on Wednesday, John Bainton, of Manchester, was charged with breaking open the cffertory box at the Catholic Chapel.—Father Barry's servant girl said she was dusting the edifice when the prisoner entered. She looked at him, and he made use of a foul expression and walked out. Perceiving him coming in a second time, she concealed her- self and watched his movements. After looking carefully round, he broke open the offertory box, took the money, and made off. Witness informed her master of the theft, and he followed the prisoner and gave him into custody. A police- man's dog was subsequently taken to a street where some of the money was suppose to be hidden, and ordered by signs to find it. The animal stopped at a 0. rtain spot, and some stones being removed, is. 101 d. was' found there. It ap- peared that a box of another church near had been found broken into, and the sexton now identified the prisoner as one of four men (also in custody) who were seen in the church on Saturday.—Prisoner was remanded.

div.head: LUNCHEON.
div.p: LUNCHEON.

The luncheon was held in a large tent, and was splendidly served, under the superintendence of Mr. Dove. Mr. A. B. Walker, president of the society, presided, and amongst those by whom he was supported were the Revs. George Holloway, vic ir of Farnworth ; Thomas Chambers, vicar of Halewood; Sir R. A. Cross, M.P.; Major Cross, and Mr. R. Whalley. _
, The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were proposed by the Chairman.

The Rev. GEO. HOLLOWAY responded on behalf of "The bishop and clergy, and ministers of all denominations." Immediately before this, the CITAIRMiN called for three cheers for Sir R. A. Cross, who was obliged to leave. [The cheers with were given great heartiness.] Sir R. A. CROSS said he was truly glad to be with them that day, but he was compelled to leave the meeting in order to meet a train to convey him to a place where he was obliged be present that night. In saying good bye to them he wished them all prosperity. Let them keep up hearts, for he was convinced there was a very good future before them as agriculturalists, if they would only go at their work, as he believed they would, as Lancashire men. (Applause.) Major qROSS (chairman of the Widnes Local Board), in acknowledging the toast of "The army, navy, and volun- teers," said he felt highly honoured by having his name coupled with it. He need say nothing concerning the army and navy, who had earned the thanks of all true Britons. The volunteers were beginning to prove they were a power in the country, and a power which he was sure would always be exercised for good. Whilst upon his feet, he might as well congratulate that large meeting on the tine weather that had now set in, and which, in the judgment of most present, must be worth a very great deal in enabling the farmers to save their crops. He was sure that the beau- tiful weather they were having must be worth millions of money to the whole country; and he hoped it might con- tinue for some time longer, and so let everything be done properly to make a happy ending to what had been the be- ginning of an unfortunate harvest. (Applause). Colonel BLACIMURNE, M.P., who was received with loud cheers, said he was present as a landlord and tenant farmer to meet them all under circumstances which called for con- siderable rejoicing, for they had sunshine of a most brilliant character, and hopes that the remainder of the harvest would be as good as possible. (Hear, hear.) He was alsc present as one of their county members, and he came amongst them with the greatest pleasure. He, however, lamentad extremely the absence of his distinguished col- league. The fact was that the gentleman in question had been doing a great deal of work lately, and it was absolutely necessary that he should leave that gathering in order to be present that night at a particular place in the very north of Lancashire. The following week Sir R. Cross would be in the neighbourhood again in order to perform a particular duty which he hoped might prove of great benefit to the large community in which it would take place. He therefore hoped that Mr. Cross would be excused for leaving them upon that particular occasion. He (the speaker) was also

div.head: TERRIBLE SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: TERRIBLE SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.

THE INQUEST. On Thursday, an inquest was held at the Town Hall, Runcorn, by T. J. Ridgway, county coroner, on the body of John Sutton, blacksmith, aged 40 years, who committed suicide on Tuesday afternoon, by blowing his head off with gunpowder. The evidence showed that deceased had for a long time been out of work and in a somewhat depressed state of mind. He had been in the habit of constantly quarrelling with his wife, and had on several occasions sold all the furniture to obtain drink. Some time ago he was sent to Knutsford for drunkenness, and the police books show that he has been there about a dozen times, though the general public appeared to have a notion that he was a very quiet sort of man. The Coroner, in summing up, said it appeared evident from the statements made by two of the witnesses, that for some time past he had not known what he was doing. The evidence pointed out that a conviction had been obtained against him for not sending his child to school, and that he had been the subject of several County Court summonses which he saw no means of paying, so that he was afraid he would be sent to gaol. Indeed it was stated that Mr. Bowyer. the attendance officer of the School Board had told him that he should be obliged to take out a warrant of commitment against him. Charlotte Sutton, wife of deceased, said that on the previous Saturday night she left him, as he was worse for drink. Deceased had not been thoroughly sober for a fortnight, and had far -rime time been constitutionally weak. She returned home about nine o'clock en Sunday night, and he asked her where she had been. He had had some beer, but not very much. On the Sunday he sold a pair of scales, in order to obtain drink. On Monday morning she left home to go washing, and returned about nine o'clock at night. In the evening she heard deceased was at the Albion beerhouse, in Nelson-street, and she called there and saw he was drunk. She asked him if it was not time for him to come home, and he asked her what his being there had to do with her, and used bad language. He added that he would put her another patch on her face—one that would neither draw blood nor matter. Slim then went to her mother's. About half-past one she went back again, and observed that some things were missing from the fire place, including an ash- pan and a jockey-bar. Sims and her daughter went to several places to find Ler hatiband, and they ultimately discovered him at the house of a Mrs. Doyle, who told her st • had bought the jockey-bar and ash-pan for od. Her husband haera very wild appearance, and looked the worse for drink, very pale, wretched, and violent. She asked him why he heel sold the things, and remarked that if he had disposed of them for bread to give his children it would have been a different matter. He said, "There will be more ructiens' before this nightie over." She replied that however matters went they could not be much worse. She understood him to mean that he would dare to break up her home, as he had done on several occasions. He then went out of the house, and she bought the things back from the woman, and told her daughter not let him see them, as it might irritate him. She overtook deceased at the corner of Brunswick- street, and he got hold of her by the throat and said "Christ you." She then went home, and whilst in the kitchen heard him pulling the mattress off the bed. He then came down stairs, and told her at the bottom to go out of his way. He ran at her with an old screw driver, but she managed to get away. He tried to strike her again, but she got out of his reach, and he then came to the door and said he would knock her ether eye up, using bad language. She told him that if lie did so she should try to hurt him. He then seized a stool and threw it at her. It missed her, but struck her daughter, whom he also followed down the street with a paving stone. She did not see him again alive. About five or ten minutes afterwards, whilst in a neighbour's house, she heard a report in her own dwelling, as if a pistol or cannon had been fired. The neighbour remarked to her that it was a great shame the lads should be allowed to fire things off in such a manner. Her boy came to her imme- diately after and said the powder had been let off in her bei room. The neighbours got round the door, but some of them dissuaded her from going up stairs, as they were afraid deceased had a pistol and would fire it at her. One of the women crept up stairs and saw deceased upon the floor. She then fainted away. He had not worked regularly from the 13th October, two years ago. He had not worked at all during the present year. He had for some time been very ill and fallen away dreadfully of late. Work had also been very slack, and, of course, owing to his being a drunken man, he had injured his character. He had drunk all that he could get hold of lately, and had threatened to take his life away several times. There were a School Board summons and a rate which required to be paid, and she supposed deceased must have thought he would have to go to prison as she could not pay it He was much in debt. Last August twelve- months he went to Knutsford, and had never appeared to have any sense since. He had been in the habit of making senseless remarks, and when he had a drop of drink he had gone on like a madman, and acted in a very wild manner. He had threatened several times to take her life and those of the children. About three weeks ago, at about four o'clock in the morning, she "felt very curious" and went upstairs, and saw him standing with the razor in his hand. She then d-opped on the stairs, and he said "Weil, go upstairs again" and put the razor in the cupboard. On a night afterwards she found the razor under her own pillow. Deceased had not been sober any whole day for a long time.—Eliza Ellis, wife of Wm Ellis, Nelson-street, said that about twenty to twelve, on Tuesday morning, deceased came to her house and borrowed a comb, which he returned in a few minutes and said "You will hear a noise in my house in a short time." Some few minutes after he wished to borrow a pair of pincers, but she professed she could not find them, as she fancied he wished to take down the bed to sell it. He looked very wild, and as if he did not know what he was doing. He had orrowed a razor from her several times to shave himself. —Mrs. Ellen EN ans, wife of Thomas Evans, Nelson-street, spoke to the drunaen character of the deceased. She also stated that she was convinced he had been in a very de- pressed state owing to fearing that he would be sent to gaol under the conviction that had been obtained against him by the School Board.—Mr. Yarwood, one of the jury, said that in former years he always considered the deceased a very steady man.—P.C. Kelley said that about two o'clock on Tuesday afternoon, he and Sergeant Hollingworth were called to the deceased's house. He found deceased lying dead upon a mattrass in the bedroom, with his face and top jaw blown off. He searched the room and found some pow- der in a paper under deceased's face. His left hand was black. There were also a half burned match near him. There were some bills and county court papers in the room. He could not find where the powder had been purchased.—Mrs. Mary Cooke, wife of John Cook, Nelson-street. said she had known deceased 17 years. He had for sometime been very depressed. He was very excitable when under the influence of drink.—John Waterworth, licensed victualler, of the Boat House Inn, proved that on the day of his death the deceased came to his house arid spent sixpence in drink. Deceased seemed in very fair spirits.— The Coroner then sunned up, and said that deceased evidently appeared to have lived a most wretched life for some time. It seemed from the evidence of two of the wit- nesses as if for some time past the deceased had not lived a regular life.—The jury then retired to consider their verdict, but after an hour's consideration they could not come to any decision.—The Coroner was again called into the room, and sent for Mr. Lea, who was examined as to whether he had sold any powder to deceased. He said he might have obtained it at the shop, but he could not say clearly. He then gave evidence as to the different effects dynamite and Powder would have in such a case.—The jury, after three boars' deliberation, returned a verdict to the effect that deceased committed suicide whilst in a state of temporaty insanity. 13,

OVER AGRICULTURAL SILGIW.—OG Saturday last, this annual show was held at Over. The attendance was not up to what was anticipated, but this might be owing to the dull and somewhat threatening weather more than to the failing interest. The number of entries, between 350 and 400, shows that it holds its sway among the neighbouring farmers, arc., if entries are any evidence apart from public support. The President for this year is Lord Cole, M.P., but in his absence the Vice-President, Lord Delamere, kept up the interest of ' the society, in which his lordship is fittingly supported by several other vice-presidents, as Lord Leigh, Mr. Knowles, M.P.. Captain Turner, Mr. 11. E. Falk, Mr. G. F. Wilbraham, Mr. J. Brunner, and a committee consisting of the chief farmers within a radius of several miles. Tho following gentlemen acted as judges :—Cattle, Mr. Smith and Mr. Parr; horses, light, Colonel Cliolmondley and Captain Tomkinson ; horses, heavy, Mr. Wm. Whitlow and Mr. Barker; butter and che,se, Mr. Hall; pigs, cheese, and farm produce, Mr. C. Davies and Mr. Hopkins; poultry, Mr. Pierce; veterinary surgeon, Mr. Fryer. Of horned cattle there was a better show, both in number and Quality, than formerly. Of horses, for agricultural purposes, few entries were made, but of mares some dozen Or more, all excellent types. Leaping called forth, as usual, much interest, but one of the greatest favourites, Mr. W. Cossins, was unfor- tunately thrown and hurt, which acted as a damper. Turn- outs excited attention and comment, and much praise was lavished generally. Pigs were plentifully shown, and some were specially good. Cheese and butter stood well and claim- ed much notice, lithe entries were but few for the former. Poultry of every variety made a good show, and farm pro- duce was abundantly represented. The cottage farmers came in for their share of commendation and reward which like all the above on a larger scale has it local bearing and interest which should alike redound to the suppoit and per- petuity of the society so fostering excellence. A public dinner served at MrlHopley's, the Wheat, Sheaf and preisded over by Lord Delamere was well attended. After due justice had been done to the excellent catering of Mr. Holey, and the usual loyal toasts from the chair, the following toasts were honoured likewise, "Army, navy, and volunteers," by Mr. H. E. Falk, which Colonel Cholmondley, and W. H. Verden replied to both, eulogizing the regular and reserve forces as well as the navy, and believing in the firm support they would all render Her Majesty if needed. Lord Dela- mere proposed success to "Over Agricultural Society," and in doing so, spoke of the agricultural depression and Free Trade which are so prominently before the English mind at present. He believed the medium between Flee Trade and Protection would be found nearest right.--Dr. Okell replied, adverting to the great good done by the society during its quarter of a century of existence, and Co the likelihood of an amalgamation with neighbouring societies-Dr. Morton gave the health of the "Judges," especially referring to 31r. Tomkinson, who replied in a manly speech.--Itr.Gr.E. Wilbraham proposed the health of the "President, to whichs Lord Delamere responded ; as did Mr. Gartit, to the oat of his health, by Mr. Smallwood..—The Secretary believed that b several small societies could, with advantage, e amalga- mated. This brought the proceedings to a close.

WARRINGTON UNlON.—Persons willing to CON- TRACT for the Supply of any of the undermentioned articles, from Michaelmas to Lady-day next. to be delivered free of expense at the Warrington Union Workhouse, or if required at the Industrial Schools, Wilson-Patten-street, at such times and in such quantities as the Board of Guardians shall direct, are requested to send in TENDERS properly sealed, endorsed, and free of expense, addressed to the Clerk to the Guardians, before four o'clock p.m. on Tuesday, the 20th day or September instant. The following are the articles for which Tenders are required:— Groceries and Provisions I Beef and Mutton Milk and Butter I Beer and Porter Flour and Meal Wines and Spirits Coal and Slack Drapery, Sze. Straw and Potatoes Shoes and Clogs Suits of Clothes Glazing Shaving and Haircutting Coffins Best Oakum rope for picking Brushes Best Australian Beef Best Cheshire Cheese Loaves of Bread for schools. Samples of any of the above may be seen on application to the Master of the Workhouse. Forms of tender and full particulars as tst the probable quantities ot each article requires:lnlay be obtained at the Clerk's office. The Guardians also invite Tenders for the supply of Printing and Stationery, from Michaelmas, 1881, to Michaelmas, 1882. All goods under this head must be equal to sample, to be seen at the Clerk's office, where also forms of Tender, Ecc., may be obtained. Each tender must be made upon the prescribed form and properly enclosed, and endorsed with the name of the article tendered for. Each contractor must be prepared (if required) to enter into security for the due performance of his contract. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any Tender. All contract accounts will be paid quarterly, upon delivery of statement.—By order, JAMES CLOWES SUTTON, Clerk to the Guardians. Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, September 10th, 1881.

RUNCORN UNION.—CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the half-year ending, 29th March, 1882.—The GUARDIANS of the POOR of the RUNCORN UNION are desir•us of receiving TENDERS from parties willing to CON- TRACT for the supply of Flour and Oatmeal, Groceries, Peas, Cheese, Bait Butter ; Cod Liver and Paraffin 011 ; Quinine ; good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price to include about 301bs. per week of the best butcher's meat for the officers, and sides of Mutton; beat brand (lets) American Bacon; Potatoes; Wheat Straw; Drapery and Clothing; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples, to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; House Coal (colliery to be named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size of each, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile, and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except drapery goods) as far 1 as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsharn, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other c3n be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles requlred and further particulars may be obtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwarded to the Clerk's office, Frodsham, on or before SATURDAY, the Ist day of October, 1881, endorsed "Tender for . ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guar- dians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 4th October, 1881, at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter Into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians. By order of the Board, H. LINAKER, FroJsham, 6th September, 1881. Clerk to the Guardians
